Plant data, makers' documents, or measurements supplied by the user take the place of the list's ranges for that case.

For teaching. The entries can be used as spotting exercises: give the best-attempt solution without the doubt paragraphs, and require the weakness to be found and the settling check to be named. Spotting the weakness takes experience with built, running equipment. That is itself one of the list's findings.

Weak Areas Not in the List

The list covers types where a best numerical attempt and a bounded range are possible. Other areas are also weak and sit outside the list, because no such range can be given: plant layout and spacing; human error and how far set procedures can be trusted; upkeep and inspection planning beyond entry F3; buying and judging suppliers; the order of building work; reading rules and laws for a place and date; and any question that rests on the current edition of a restricted code, a live price, or the state of one named unit. Absence from Parts A to G does not mean the model is strong in these areas.

Closing note. The weaknesses recorded here come from the facts open to the model, and from the form in which chemical engineering knowledge is published, kept restricted, or held as experience. The list should change slowly: more computing and checks by other models act on arithmetic and on reasoning slips, and act only weakly on missing data, copied values, and unstated conventions (the unwritten rules behind a number). The list should be revised when an entry's check can be met as a matter of routine from public sources, or when measured error rates appear.

Appendix C. Method of the Study

How the Defensive Prompts Were Made

The list in Parts A to G came first. Each entry was built the same way: a problem was set, the best answer that could be given was worked out, and the answer was then pulled apart to find where it could go wrong. The weak points fell into three kinds. Some were number errors that grow as a calculation runs. Some were wrong choices of method, where a simple rule is used outside the ground where it holds. Some were missing facts, where the problem as stated does not say enough to fix one answer.

For each weak point, a prompt was written to guard against it. A defensive prompt is a prompt written with the weakness named in it: it tells the AI agent to state the weak point, to give a range instead of one number, to say which facts are given and which are guessed, to name the missing facts instead of filling them in silently, and to check the answer by a second route. The prompt for each entry stands at the end of that entry, and the shared prompts stand in Appendix B.

The prompts were then turned into standing rules: the seven shared guards were written into the saved rules that every AI agent in this workspace works under, so the guards were in force for every answer, whether the person asking knew about the list or not. The first blind test (below) ran under those standing rules, with tool use allowed as well. Tool use and the rules were in force at the same time, so that test cannot show how much of its result came from each.

A second test was therefore run with the prompt as the only difference between its two halves. Before it ran, every rule and note learned from the first study was taken out of the saved files the agents start from, and a test agent with a fresh start confirmed that none of that material was present. The files were restored unchanged after the test, and a second test agent confirmed the material was back.

This loop is a form of recursive self-improvement. The word recursive means that the output of a round feeds back into the next round. The AI agent studied its own weak points, wrote the study down, turned the study into rules and prompts for its own later work, and was then tested on the same problems under controlled conditions. The limits of the claim are stated in Section 3.

The Blind Tests

First test. Each of the 32 problems was given to a fresh AI agent (Muse Spark 1.3). The agent received the problem text only. It did not receive the list, the ranges in the list, or the scoring rules, and it was not told that a test was taking place. Each agent could use tools, including a program for running calculations and web search, and the standing defensive rules described above were in force. Each agent tried once. The answers were not edited.

Second test. Sixty-four fresh agents were used, two per problem. One agent of each pair received the problem text only. The other received the same problem text plus that entry's defensive prompt, word for word, as an added instruction. Tool use was open to both halves, so the prompt was the only difference between the halves. The standing rules from the first study were not in force for either half (see above). Each agent tried once. The answers were not edited.

Scoring. Each answer was scored with three questions. Question 1: did the answer's main number fall inside the range printed in the list for that problem? Inside the range counts as a pass; outside counts as a miss, even if the number is near the range. An answer that gave no main number, because it held the problem to be underdetermined, is recorded as "no value" and counted separately from a miss. Question 2: did the answer warn about doubt, by giving a range, by naming a missing fact, or by naming the check that would settle the question? In the second test, an answer in the prompted half whose warning only repeated the words of its prompt, without applying them to the problem, was scored as repeating, not warning. Question 3: did the answer use a sensible method, rather than a weak shortcut, such as treating a high-pressure gas as an ideal gas? Answers were also checked for signs that the agent had found or used the published list. No answer in either test showed any such sign, so no answer was set aside.

Appendix D. The Test Responses in Full

The 64 responses of the second blind test, reproduced in full and unedited; only the rendering has been converted for this page, and the notation in each response is its author's own. For every problem, the response without defensive prompting stands first and the response with defensive prompting second. The scores for these responses are the table in Section 2.

A1. Henry's Law Conventions

Response without defensive prompt

Equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration in water at 25 °C in contact with air

Given data
  • Partial pressure of oxygen, denoted pp, in atmospheres (atm): p=0.21 atmp = 0.21\ \text{atm}
  • Solubility-form Henry constant, denoted kHk_H, in moles per litre per atmosphere (mol/(L·atm)): kH=1.3×10−3 mol/(L⋅atm)k_H = 1.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol/(L·atm)}
  • Molar mass of oxygen, denoted MM, in grams per mole (g/mol): M=32 g/molM = 32\ \text{g/mol}
  • Temperature: 25 ∘C25\ ^\circ\text{C} (the stated value of kHk_H applies at this temperature)
Method

For a dilute solution in equilibrium with a gas, Henry's law in solubility form gives the equilibrium liquid-phase molar concentration, denoted CC, in moles per litre (mol/L), as

C=kH pC = k_H \, p

Substitution of the given values gives CC, and multiplication by MM converts the molar concentration to a mass concentration, denoted CmC_m, in milligrams per litre (mg/L).

Calculation

Molar concentration:

C=kH p=(1.3×10−3 molL⋅atm)(0.21 atm)=2.73×10−4 molLC = k_H \, p = \left(1.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \frac{\text{mol}}{\text{L·atm}}\right)(0.21\ \text{atm}) = 2.73 \times 10^{-4}\ \frac{\text{mol}}{\text{L}}

The units check: (mol/(L·atm)) × atm = mol/L, as required.

Mass concentration:

Cm=C M=(2.73×10−4 molL)(32 gmol)=8.736×10−3 gLC_m = C \, M = \left(2.73 \times 10^{-4}\ \frac{\text{mol}}{\text{L}}\right)\left(32\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{mol}}\right) = 8.736 \times 10^{-3}\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}

Since 1 g/L=1000 mg/L1\ \text{g/L} = 1000\ \text{mg/L}:

Cm=8.736×10−3 gL×1000 mgg=8.7 mg/LC_m = 8.736 \times 10^{-3}\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}} \times 1000\ \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{g}} = 8.7\ \text{mg/L}

Result

The equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration in water at 25 ∘C25\ ^\circ\text{C} in contact with air is

  • C=2.7×10−4 mol/LC = 2.7 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol/L}, or equivalently
  • Cm≈8.7 mg/LC_m \approx 8.7\ \text{mg/L}

This value is consistent with the commonly reported saturation dissolved-oxygen concentration of about 88–9 mg/L9\ \text{mg/L} for water in equilibrium with air at 25 ∘C25\ ^\circ\text{C} and 1 atm1\ \text{atm} total pressure.

Response with defensive prompt

Equilibrium Dissolved-Oxygen Concentration in Water at 25 °C

Given data and definitions
  • The temperature, denoted TT, in degrees Celsius (°C), is T=25 °CT = 25\ \text{°C}.
  • The partial pressure of oxygen in the air in contact with the water, denoted pp, in atmospheres (atm), is p=0.21 atmp = 0.21\ \text{atm}.
  • The solubility-form Henry constant for oxygen in water at 25 °C, denoted kHk_{\mathrm{H}}, in moles per litre per atmosphere (mol/(L·atm)), is kH=1.3×10−3 mol/(L⋅atm)k_{\mathrm{H}} = 1.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol/(L·atm)}.
  • The molar mass of oxygen, denoted MM, in grams per mole (g/mol), is M=32 g/molM = 32\ \text{g/mol}.
  • The equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration on a molar basis, denoted cc, in moles per litre (mol/L), is the quantity to be determined.
  • The equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration on a mass basis, denoted cmc_{\mathrm{m}}, in milligrams per litre (mg/L), is obtained from cc and MM.
Henry's law convention used

The convention used is the solubility form of Henry's law: at fixed temperature, the equilibrium concentration of a dissolved gas is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid, and the constant of proportionality is the solubility-form Henry constant.

In an equation, with units stated:

c [mol/L]=kH [mol/(L⋅atm)]×p [atm]c\ [\text{mol/L}] = k_{\mathrm{H}}\ [\text{mol/(L·atm)}] \times p\ [\text{atm}]

A larger value of kHk_{\mathrm{H}} in this convention therefore means a more soluble gas. This convention is not the inverse volatility form, in which the partial pressure is written as proportional to the dissolved mole fraction; that inverse form is not used here.

Calculation

Substitution of kHk_{\mathrm{H}} and pp into the equation above gives:

c=(1.3×10−3 mol/(L⋅atm))×(0.21 atm)c = (1.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol/(L·atm)}) \times (0.21\ \text{atm})

The unit atm cancels:

c=2.73×10−4 mol/Lc = 2.73 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol/L}

Conversion to a mass basis uses MM, with the conversion factor of 1000 milligrams per gram, denoted as 1000 mg/g1000\ \text{mg/g} in the equation below:

cm=c×M×1000 mg/gc_{\mathrm{m}} = c \times M \times 1000\ \text{mg/g}

cm=(2.73×10−4 mol/L)×(32 g/mol)×(1000 mg/g)c_{\mathrm{m}} = (2.73 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol/L}) \times (32\ \text{g/mol}) \times (1000\ \text{mg/g})

The unit mol cancels between cc and MM, and the unit g cancels with the conversion factor:

cm=8.736 mg/L≈8.7 mg/Lc_{\mathrm{m}} = 8.736\ \text{mg/L} \approx 8.7\ \text{mg/L}

Result

The equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration in water at 25 °C in contact with air is:

  • c=2.7×10−4 mol/Lc = 2.7 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol/L} (to two significant figures, matching the two significant figures in kHk_{\mathrm{H}} and pp), or equivalently
  • cm≈8.7 mg/Lc_{\mathrm{m}} \approx 8.7\ \text{mg/L}.
Verification against a known saturation concentration

The known saturation concentration of dissolved oxygen in fresh water at 25 °C in contact with air at a total pressure of 1 atm is approximately 8.3 mg/L8.3\ \text{mg/L}, as tabulated in standard dissolved-oxygen solubility tables (for example, the Engineering ToolBox table of oxygen solubility in fresh water: 258 μmol/L258\ \mu\text{mol/L}, equal to 8.3 mg/L8.3\ \text{mg/L}, at 25 °C and 760 mm Hg).

Comparison:

  • Calculated value: 8.7 mg/L8.7\ \text{mg/L}
  • Tabulated value: 8.3 mg/L8.3\ \text{mg/L}
  • Difference: 8.7−8.3=0.4 mg/L8.7 - 8.3 = 0.4\ \text{mg/L}, approximately 5%5\% of the tabulated value

Agreement within approximately 5%5\% is consistent with the precision of the inputs: kHk_{\mathrm{H}} and pp are each given to only two significant figures, and p=0.21 atmp = 0.21\ \text{atm} takes no account of water vapour reducing the oxygen partial pressure in air saturated with water vapour. The calculated result therefore verifies against the known saturation concentration.

Scope

The result applies to dilute, fresh water at equilibrium with air at 25 °C, with no oxygen consumption or production in the water, no salinity correction, and no supersaturation.

A2. Non-Ideal Vapour–Liquid Equilibrium

Response without defensive prompt

Bubble-Point Pressure for a Strongly Non-Ideal Binary Liquid

Definitions
  • PP is the bubble-point pressure, in kilopascals (kPa), to be determined.
  • TT is the fixed temperature, in kelvin (K); a numerical value is not required for the conclusion.
  • x1x_1 is the liquid mole fraction of component 1, dimensionless, with x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40.
  • x2x_2 is the liquid mole fraction of component 2, dimensionless.
  • y1y_1 is the vapour mole fraction of component 1, dimensionless.
  • y2y_2 is the vapour mole fraction of component 2, dimensionless.
  • P1satP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} is the pure-component vapour pressure of component 1 at TT, in kilopascals (kPa), with P1sat=120 kPaP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 120\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • P2satP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} is the pure-component vapour pressure of component 2 at TT, in kilopascals (kPa), with P2sat=50 kPaP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} = 50\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • γ1\gamma_1 is the liquid-phase activity coefficient of component 1 at TT and at the stated liquid composition, dimensionless.
  • γ2\gamma_2 is the liquid-phase activity coefficient of component 2 at TT and at the stated liquid composition, dimensionless.
Governing relation

The second liquid mole fraction follows from the mole-fraction sum:

x2=1−x1=1−0.40=0.60.x_2 = 1 - x_1 = 1 - 0.40 = 0.60.

For a vapour phase treated as an ideal gas and a non-ideal liquid, the modified Raoult relation for each component states that the component partial pressure in the vapour equals the liquid mole fraction multiplied by the activity coefficient and by the pure-component vapour pressure. Summation over both components, with y1+y2=1y_1 + y_2 = 1, gives

P=x1γ1P1sat+x2γ2P2sat.P = x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} + x_2 \gamma_2 P_2^{\mathrm{sat}}.

Substitution of the stated values gives

P=(0.40)(γ1)(120 kPa)+(0.60)(γ2)(50 kPa),P = (0.40)(\gamma_1)(120\ \mathrm{kPa}) + (0.60)(\gamma_2)(50\ \mathrm{kPa}),

P=48 γ1+30 γ2kPa,P = 48\,\gamma_1 + 30\,\gamma_2 \quad \mathrm{kPa},

where the numerical coefficients 48 and 30 carry units of kilopascals (kPa).

The corresponding vapour composition, if values of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 were supplied, would follow from

y1=x1γ1P1satP=48 γ1P,y_1 = \frac{x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}}}{P} = \frac{48\,\gamma_1}{P},

with PP inserted in kilopascals (kPa) in the final ratio.

Determination from the stated data

No numerical value of γ1\gamma_1 or γ2\gamma_2 is given, and no activity-coefficient model or model parameters are given from which γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 could be calculated at x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40. No experimental vapour–liquid equilibrium point, azeotropic composition, or azeotropic pressure is given. The description "strongly non-ideal" states that γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 differ appreciably from unity, without stating the direction or the magnitude of the deviation for either component.

The quantity PP is therefore not determined by the stated data. The following admissible cases, each consistent with every stated value, demonstrate the non-uniqueness. The values in the table are illustrative activity coefficients at the stated composition, not predictions for a named mixture.

Case γ1\gamma_1 γ2\gamma_2 P=48 γ1+30 γ2P = 48\,\gamma_1 + 30\,\gamma_2 (kPa) y1y_1
Ideal reference, γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1 1.0 1.0 78 0.615
Positive deviation, γ1=γ2=2\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 2 2.0 2.0 156 0.615
Negative deviation, γ1=γ2=0.5\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 0.5 0.5 0.5 39 0.615
Unequal deviation 3.0 1.5 189 0.762

A positive deviation raises PP above the ideal reference value; a negative deviation lowers PP below that value; unequal values of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 also change y1y_1. A single numerical pressure cannot be selected from these cases without additional information.

Reference value under an ideal-liquid assumption

If, contrary to the stated strong non-ideality, the liquid were ideal, then γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1 and

Pideal=48+30=78 kPa,P_{\mathrm{ideal}} = 48 + 30 = 78\ \mathrm{kPa},

where PidealP_{\mathrm{ideal}} is the bubble-point pressure under the ideal-liquid assumption, in kilopascals (kPa). The corresponding ideal vapour composition is

y1=4878=0.615.y_1 = \frac{48}{78} = 0.615.

The value 78 kPa78\ \mathrm{kPa} is a reference value only. It is not an estimate for the stated strongly non-ideal liquid, because the assumption used to obtain it contradicts the problem statement.

Conclusion

The bubble-point pressure cannot be estimated uniquely from x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40, P1sat=120 kPaP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 120\ \mathrm{kPa}, and P2sat=50 kPaP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} = 50\ \mathrm{kPa} alone. The determinable result is

P=48 γ1+30 γ2kPa.P = 48\,\gamma_1 + 30\,\gamma_2 \quad \mathrm{kPa}.

A numerical result requires, at minimum, one of the following at TT and at x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40:

  1. measured or correlated values of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2; or
  2. an identified activity-coefficient model (for example, a Margules, van Laar, Wilson, or non-random two-liquid model) together with its numerical parameters for the named pair of components at TT; or
  3. experimental vapour–liquid equilibrium data for the named mixture from which γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 can be obtained.

At elevated pressure, vapour-phase fugacity coefficients and a liquid molar-volume (Poynting) correction would also be required; those corrections are secondary to the missing activity coefficients, which alone prevent a numerical answer here.

Response with defensive prompt

Bubble-Point Pressure of a Strongly Non-Ideal Binary Liquid

Symbols and given data
  • PP — bubble-point pressure, in kilopascals (kPa); the quantity sought.
  • x1x_1 — liquid mole fraction of component 1, dimensionless; x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40.
  • x2x_2 — liquid mole fraction of component 2, dimensionless; x2=1−x1=0.60x_2 = 1 - x_1 = 0.60.
  • P1satP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} — pure-component vapour pressure of component 1 at the fixed temperature, in kPa; P1sat=120 kPaP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 120\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • P2satP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} — pure-component vapour pressure of component 2 at the fixed temperature, in kPa; P2sat=50 kPaP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} = 50\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • γ1\gamma_1, γ2\gamma_2 — liquid-phase activity coefficients of components 1 and 2, dimensionless; γi=1\gamma_i = 1 for an ideal solution (where ii, the component index, is 1 or 2).
  • y1y_1 — vapour mole fraction of component 1 at the bubble point, dimensionless.
  • A12A_{12}, A21A_{21} — dimensionless binary interaction parameters of an activity-coefficient model, defined by the model equations in which they first appear below.
Governing equation and the missing information

At low to moderate pressure, with the vapour treated as an ideal gas and the Poynting correction (the correction for the effect of pressure on liquid fugacity) neglected, the modified Raoult law gives, at the bubble point,

P=x1γ1P1sat+x2γ2P2sat,y1=x1γ1P1satP.P = x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} + x_2 \gamma_2 P_2^{\mathrm{sat}}, \qquad y_1 = \frac{x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}}}{P}.

The temperature is fixed, so P1satP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} and P2satP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} are fixed. The problem therefore reduces to γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 at x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40.

Those coefficients are not given, and they cannot be obtained from the data supplied:

  1. The components are not identified, so no measured activity-coefficient data and no fitted model parameters for the actual pair can be selected.
  2. The sign of the deviation is not stated. "Strongly non-ideal" covers γi≫1\gamma_i \gg 1 (positive deviation) and γi≪1\gamma_i \ll 1 (negative deviation).
  3. No numerical temperature, measured vapour–liquid equilibrium point, infinite-dilution activity coefficient, or excess Gibbs energy is given from which parameters could be fitted.

The ideal-solution value,

Pideal=(0.40)(120 kPa)+(0.60)(50 kPa)=78 kPa,P_{\mathrm{ideal}} = (0.40)(120\ \mathrm{kPa}) + (0.60)(50\ \mathrm{kPa}) = 78\ \mathrm{kPa},

is therefore only a reference. It is excluded by the statement that the liquid is strongly non-ideal (γi=1\gamma_i = 1 throughout in that calculation).

A defensible answer must be conditional: apply documented, strongly non-ideal model parameter sets, state their source and data range, and compare the results.

Model 1 — Positive deviation: ethanol–water parameter sets

Ethanol (component 1) + water (component 2) is a standard strongly positive-deviation system, with a minimum-boiling azeotrope at 1 atmosphere (atm), where 1 atm = 101.325 kPa.

Model 1a — Three-suffix Margules equation

The three-suffix Margules equations are

ln⁡γ1=x22[A12+2(A21−A12)x1],ln⁡γ2=x12[A21+2(A12−A21)x2].\ln \gamma_1 = x_2^{2}\left[A_{12} + 2\left(A_{21} - A_{12}\right) x_1\right], \qquad \ln \gamma_2 = x_1^{2}\left[A_{21} + 2\left(A_{12} - A_{21}\right) x_2\right].

Parameter source and data range: A12=1.6022A_{12} = 1.6022 and A21=0.7947A_{21} = 0.7947, the ethanol–water values attributed to Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook and used in the Smith, Van Ness, Abbott and Swihart textbook treatment. The underlying data are isobaric (constant-pressure) vapour–liquid equilibrium data at approximately 101.3 kPa over the full composition range 0≤x1≤10 \le x_1 \le 1, between the pure boiling temperatures of ethanol (about 78 ∘C78\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}) and water (100 ∘C100\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}). Transferring the parameters to the unspecified temperature at which the stated vapour pressures occur is an approximation; activity-coefficient parameters vary with temperature.

At x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40, x2=0.60x_2 = 0.60:

  • ln⁡γ1=0.344\ln \gamma_1 = 0.344, so γ1=1.41\gamma_1 = 1.41.
  • ln⁡γ2=0.282\ln \gamma_2 = 0.282, so γ2=1.33\gamma_2 = 1.33.
  • P=(0.40)(1.41)(120)+(0.60)(1.33)(50)=67.7+39.8=107.5 kPaP = (0.40)(1.41)(120) + (0.60)(1.33)(50) = 67.7 + 39.8 = 107.5\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • y1=67.7/107.5=0.63y_1 = 67.7 / 107.5 = 0.63.
Model 1b — van Laar equation, same system

The van Laar equations are

ln⁡γ1=A12[A21x2A12x1+A21x2]2,ln⁡γ2=A21[A12x1A12x1+A21x2]2.\ln \gamma_1 = A_{12}\left[\frac{A_{21} x_2}{A_{12} x_1 + A_{21} x_2}\right]^{2}, \qquad \ln \gamma_2 = A_{21}\left[\frac{A_{12} x_1}{A_{12} x_1 + A_{21} x_2}\right]^{2}.

Parameter source and data range: A12=1.6798A_{12} = 1.6798 and A21=0.9227A_{21} = 0.9227, the recommended ethanol–water values in Gmehling, Onken and Arlt, Vapor–Liquid Equilibrium Data Collection (DECHEMA Chemistry Data Series), obtained by regression of measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data over the full composition range 0≤x1≤10 \le x_1 \le 1 at near-atmospheric conditions. A separate regression of isobaric ethanol–water data at 101.3 kPa (Bakir et al., Journal of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, 2010) gives similar values, A12=1.6939A_{12} = 1.6939 and A21=0.9076A_{21} = 0.9076 for the van Laar equation and A12=1.6432A_{12} = 1.6432 and A21=0.6923A_{21} = 0.6923 for the Margules equation.

At x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40, x2=0.60x_2 = 0.60:

  • ln⁡γ1=0.343\ln \gamma_1 = 0.343, so γ1=1.41\gamma_1 = 1.41.
  • ln⁡γ2=0.277\ln \gamma_2 = 0.277, so γ2=1.32\gamma_2 = 1.32.
  • P=(0.40)(1.41)(120)+(0.60)(1.32)(50)=67.6+39.6=107.2 kPaP = (0.40)(1.41)(120) + (0.60)(1.32)(50) = 67.6 + 39.6 = 107.2\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • y1=0.63y_1 = 0.63.

Models 1a and 1b agree to within 1 %. For a specified system, the choice between these two model forms is not the main uncertainty.

Model 2 — Negative deviation: acetone–chloroform, van Laar equation

Acetone (component 1) + chloroform (component 2) is a standard strongly negative-deviation system. Unlike interactions (a hydrogen bond between chloroform and acetone) are stronger than the average of the like interactions, and the system forms a maximum-boiling azeotrope at 1 atm.

Model: the van Laar equations stated in Model 1b, with the same form and symbol definitions.

Parameter source and data range: A12=−0.8643A_{12} = -0.8643 and A21=−0.5899A_{21} = -0.5899, the recommended acetone–chloroform values in the same Gmehling, Onken and Arlt DECHEMA collection cited in Model 1b, obtained by regression of measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data over the full composition range 0≤x1≤10 \le x_1 \le 1 at near-atmospheric conditions.

At x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40, x2=0.60x_2 = 0.60:

  • ln⁡γ1=−0.221\ln \gamma_1 = -0.221, so γ1=0.80\gamma_1 = 0.80.
  • ln⁡γ2=−0.144\ln \gamma_2 = -0.144, so γ2=0.87\gamma_2 = 0.87.
  • P=(0.40)(0.80)(120)+(0.60)(0.87)(50)=38.5+26.0=64.5 kPaP = (0.40)(0.80)(120) + (0.60)(0.87)(50) = 38.5 + 26.0 = 64.5\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • y1=38.5/64.5=0.60y_1 = 38.5 / 64.5 = 0.60.

Acetone (component 1) + water (component 2) shows positive deviation larger than ethanol–water, and is included to show the spread within positive-deviation systems alone.

Parameter source and data range: A12=2.1041A_{12} = 2.1041 and A21=1.5555A_{21} = 1.5555, the recommended acetone–water values in the same Gmehling, Onken and Arlt DECHEMA collection cited in Model 1b, from measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data over the full composition range 0≤x1≤10 \le x_1 \le 1 at near-atmospheric conditions.

  • ln⁡γ2=0.350\ln \gamma_2 = 0.350, so γ2=1.42\gamma_2 = 1.42.

A3. Reactive Absorption Capacity

Response without defensive prompt

Solvent circulation for carbon dioxide removal by an aqueous amine

Definitions
  • n˙CO2,abs\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2,abs}} is the molar flow rate of carbon dioxide absorbed, in kilomoles of carbon dioxide per hour (kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}).
  • α\alpha is the solvent loading, in moles of carbon dioxide per mole of amine (mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}).
  • αlean\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} is the loading of the lean solvent leaving the regenerator and entering the absorber, in mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}.
  • αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} is the loading of the rich solvent leaving the absorber, in mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}.
  • Δα\Delta\alpha is the net loading increase across the absorber, defined as Δα=αrich−αlean\Delta\alpha = \alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}, in mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}.
  • n˙amine\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} is the molar circulation rate of amine itself, in kilomoles of amine per hour (kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}). This is not the total molar, mass, or volumetric flow rate of the aqueous solution.
  • m˙solution\dot m_{\mathrm{solution}} is the mass circulation rate of the total aqueous solution, in kilograms per hour (kg h−1\mathrm{kg\,h^{-1}}).
  • V˙solution\dot V_{\mathrm{solution}} is the volumetric circulation rate of the total aqueous solution, in cubic metres per hour (m3 h−1\mathrm{m^3\,h^{-1}}).
  • MamineM_{\mathrm{amine}} is the molar mass of the amine, in kilograms per kilomole (kg kmol−1\mathrm{kg\,kmol^{-1}}).
  • waminew_{\mathrm{amine}} is the mass fraction of amine in the aqueous solution, in kilograms of amine per kilogram of solution (kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}).
  • ρsolution\rho_{\mathrm{solution}} is the density of the aqueous solution, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m−3\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}).
Given data
  • n˙CO2,abs=100 kmol h−1\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2,abs}} = 100\ \mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}
  • αlean=0.10 mol mol−1\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = 0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}

No value is given for αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}, for the amine identity, for waminew_{\mathrm{amine}}, for MamineM_{\mathrm{amine}}, or for ρsolution\rho_{\mathrm{solution}}.

Result

A unique solvent circulation rate cannot be calculated from the data given. The lean loading alone does not state how much additional carbon dioxide each mole of amine picks up in the absorber. That additional amount is Δα\Delta\alpha, and αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} is missing.

Material balance

At steady state, with amine taken as non-volatile and conserved between the lean and rich solvent streams, a carbon dioxide balance over the absorber gives

n˙amine αrich−n˙amine αlean=n˙CO2,abs\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = \dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2,abs}}

n˙amine (αrich−αlean)=n˙CO2,abs\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,(\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}) = \dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2,abs}}

n˙amine Δα=n˙CO2,abs\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,\Delta\alpha = \dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2,abs}}

Hence

n˙amine=n˙CO2,absΔα=n˙CO2,absαrich−αlean\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = \frac{\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2,abs}}}{\Delta\alpha} = \frac{\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2,abs}}}{\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}}

Substitution of the given data gives the only result supported by the statement:

n˙amine=100αrich−0.10 kmol h−1\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = \frac{100}{\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - 0.10}\ \mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}

where αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} is in mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}. A physically usable absorber requires αrich>αlean=0.10 mol mol−1\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} > \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = 0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}. As αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} approaches 0.10 mol mol−10.10\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}, Δα\Delta\alpha approaches zero and the required n˙amine\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} increases without bound.

  1. A value for αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}, or equivalently for Δα\Delta\alpha, or sufficient information to determine αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}: amine identity, absorber temperature, carbon dioxide partial pressure at the rich end of the absorber, and the equilibrium loading relation for that amine system (with any stated approach to equilibrium).
  2. The amine concentration, as waminew_{\mathrm{amine}} or an equivalent molar concentration, to convert amine circulation to total solution circulation.
  3. MamineM_{\mathrm{amine}}, fixed once the amine is named, for the mass flow rate, and ρsolution\rho_{\mathrm{solution}} at the circulation temperature if a volumetric flow rate is required.
Conclusion

The problem as stated is underdetermined. The governing sizing relation is n˙amine=100/(αrich−0.10) kmol h−1\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 100 / (\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - 0.10)\ \mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}, and no single numerical circulation rate follows until αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} (and, for the total aqueous solution flow, the amine identity and concentration) are supplied.

Response with defensive prompt

Solvent Circulation for Carbon Dioxide Removal by an Aqueous Amine

1. Given data, missing data, and consequence

Symbols are defined at first use. The loading, symbol α\alpha (unit: mol/mol), is the amount of carbon dioxide (chemical formula CO2_2) in the liquid divided by the amount of amine in the liquid, in moles of CO2_2 per mole of amine. The lean loading, symbol αL\alpha_L (unit: mol/mol), is the loading in the solvent leaving the regenerator and entering the absorber. The rich loading, symbol αR\alpha_R (unit: mol/mol), is the loading in the solvent leaving the absorber. The cyclic capacity, symbol Δα\Delta\alpha (unit: mol/mol), is αR−αL\alpha_R-\alpha_L. The molar removal rate of CO2_2, symbol n˙CO2\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} (unit: kmol/h, where kmol is kilomole and h is hour), is given as 100 kmol/h. The molar circulation rate of amine, symbol n˙amine\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} (unit: kmol/h), is the quantity to be sized.

Given, from the problem statement only:

  • n˙CO2=100 kmol/h\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 100\ \mathrm{kmol/h}, stated as a removal rate, so no separate capture fraction is applied.
  • αL=0.10 mol/mol\alpha_L = 0.10\ \mathrm{mol/mol}, stated for the lean solvent leaving the regenerator.

Not given in the problem statement:

  • the identity of the amine (for example monoethanolamine, abbreviation MEA; diethanolamine, abbreviation DEA; or methyldiethanolamine, abbreviation MDEA);
  • the amine mass fraction in the aqueous solution, symbol ww (unit: kg/kg, expressed below as wt %);
  • the absorber temperature, symbol TT (unit: °C);
  • the total pressure and the CO2_2 partial pressure in the feed gas, symbol pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} (unit: kPa, where kPa is kilopascal);
  • the treated-gas specification, the absorber approach to equilibrium, and the materials of construction.

These missing quantities determine αR\alpha_R. The equilibrium loading at the absorber bottom is the loading at which the equilibrium CO2_2 partial pressure over the loaded solution, symbol pCO2∗p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} (unit: kPa), equals pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} in the incoming gas at the absorber temperature. A real absorber must operate with pCO2∗p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} below pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} at the bottom to retain a driving force, so the operating αR\alpha_R is below the equilibrium loading at the inlet gas composition. Corrosion can impose a lower limit on αR\alpha_R than equilibrium does.

There is therefore no unique circulation rate for the problem as stated. A single numerical answer obtained from a nominal amine capacity is not defensible. The sections below give a conditional sizing on an explicitly stated benchmark solvent, with the source of every loading, the corrosion limit, an optimistic (lowest circulation) case, an equilibrium-limited case, and a conservative corrosion-limited design case. Any change of amine, concentration, temperature, or pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} requires αR\alpha_R to be taken again from vapour–liquid equilibrium data for that system.

2. Circulation balance

A steady-state CO2_2 balance over the absorber–regenerator loop, with no accumulation and no amine loss, gives

n˙CO2=n˙amine (αR−αL)=n˙amine Δα,\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,(\alpha_R-\alpha_L) = \dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,\Delta\alpha,

so that

n˙amine=n˙CO2Δα=100αR−0.10 kmol/h.\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = \frac{\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{\Delta\alpha} = \frac{100}{\alpha_R-0.10}\ \mathrm{kmol/h}.

The whole sizing question is the value of Δα\Delta\alpha. The circulation varies inversely with Δα\Delta\alpha: halving Δα\Delta\alpha doubles the circulation, and with it the pump duty, the lean–rich heat exchanger duty, and approximately the sensible-heat part of the regenerator duty.

3. Why a nominal capacity must not be used

The nominal capacity sometimes quoted for a tertiary amine is 1.0 mol/mol, from the bicarbonate stoichiometry in which one mole of amine supports one mole of CO2_2. Inserting αR=1.0\alpha_R = 1.0 mol/mol would give Δα=0.90\Delta\alpha = 0.90 mol/mol and

n˙amine=100/0.90=111 kmol/h.\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 100/0.90 = 111\ \mathrm{kmol/h}.

That result is rejected, for three reasons:

  1. For a primary or secondary amine such as MEA or DEA, the dominant product at normal loadings is the carbamate, formed by a reaction requiring two amine groups per CO2_2 molecule. The carbamate stoichiometric limit is therefore 0.5 mol/mol, not 1.0 mol/mol. Loadings above 0.5 mol/mol are reached only by carbamate hydrolysis to bicarbonate, which requires a high pCO2∗p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} (see Section 4) and is not available at low-pressure absorber conditions.
  2. A value of 1.0 mol/mol is an equilibrium limit approached only at high pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}, not an operating rich loading at the low pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} of a dilute gas.
  3. For MEA, αR=1.0\alpha_R = 1.0 mol/mol is far above the corrosion limits in Section 5 and is not an operable condition in carbon steel.

Even the carbamate value, 0.5 mol/mol, is a ceiling, not a design loading (Section 6).

4. Loadings: values and sources
4.1 Lean loading

αL=0.10\alpha_L = 0.10 mol/mol. Source: the problem statement. No equilibrium source is needed for it, because it is set by how deeply the regenerator strips the solvent, at the cost of regenerator steam.

Consistency check: 0.10 mol/mol lies at the low end of the commonly tabulated MEA operating range for the lean loading, 0.10–0.15 mol/mol (recommended ranges tabulated by Polasek and Bullin and reproduced in standard amine-plant summaries, with MEA at 15–20 wt %, rich loading 0.30–0.35 mol/mol and lean loading 0.10–0.15 mol/mol). It is deeper stripping than the 0.15–0.17 mol/mol quoted for 25–30 wt % MEA on flue gas in United States patent US 9,180,403, so it implies a higher stripping duty than that reference case. It is not a plausible lean loading for MDEA design, for which tabulated lean loadings are about 0.004–0.01 mol/mol; a lean loading of 0.10 mol/mol for MDEA would waste most of its cyclic capacity. This is a further indication that the stated lean loading is consistent with an MEA-type (primary amine) solvent, which is the benchmark adopted below. That identification is an assumption made here, not a datum of the problem.

4.2 Equilibrium rich loading for the benchmark solvent

Benchmark assumed for the equilibrium figures in this section: aqueous MEA at w=30w = 30 wt %, absorber bottom temperature T=40T = 40 °C, feed gas near atmospheric pressure with pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} in the range 4–15 kPa (0.04–0.15 atm, the flue-gas range). These are stated here as the conditions of the calculation, because the problem statement states none of them.

Primary equilibrium sources:

  • Jou, F.-Y., Mather, A. E. and Otto, F. D., "The solubility of CO2_2 in a 30 mass percent monoethanolamine solution", Canadian Journal of Chemical Engineering, 1995, 73, 140–147: the standard measured solubility data set for 30 wt % MEA over a wide range of temperature, pressure and loading.
  • Aronu, U. E. and co-workers, "Solubility of CO2_2 in 15, 30, 45 and 60 mass % MEA from 40 to 120 °C and model representation using the extended UNIQUAC framework", Chemical Engineering Science, 2011–2012: measured CO2_2 partial pressures as a function of loading for 15–60 wt % MEA at 40–120 °C.
  • Measured data for 30 wt % MEA at 40 °C tabulated in Gases, 2026, Politecnico di Milano equilibrium-unit validation study (doi:10.3390/gases6010001, where doi is digital object identifier): pCO2∗p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is about 5 kPa at α=0.42\alpha = 0.42–0.46 mol/mol and about 7 kPa at α=0.50\alpha = 0.50 mol/mol, and then rises steeply, to about 80 kPa at α=0.61\alpha = 0.61 mol/mol. The steep rise after 0.5 mol/mol is the carbamate-to-bicarbonate transition described in Section 3.

Consequences for the benchmark:

  • At pCO2≈10p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \approx 10 kPa and 40 °C, an equilibrium loading of about 0.50–0.54 mol/mol is measured in a screening apparatus at 95 % approach (benchmark validation against Hartono and co-workers, reported in Processes, 2019, 7, 160). Equilibrium alone, at this partial pressure, does not limit αR\alpha_R below the carbamate value.
  • At the lower partial pressures of a dilute gas, and after allowing a finite driving force at the absorber bottom, the attainable rich loading is lower. United States patent US 9,180,403, summarising industrial MEA practice at pCO2=0.04p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.04–0.15 atm with 25–30 wt % MEA, states a rich loading of about 0.42–0.45 mol/mol and a lean loading of about 0.15–0.17 mol/mol, i.e. a cyclic capacity of 0.25–0.30 mol/mol.
  • Rochelle and co-workers (National Petroleum Council carbon capture appendix, 2019–2021) define a consistent comparison basis by taking the rich loading as the loading giving pCO2∗=5p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 5 kPa at 40 °C and the lean loading as the loading giving pCO2∗=0.5p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.5 kPa at 40 °C. On the 40 °C data above, pCO2∗=5p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 5 kPa corresponds to αR≈0.44\alpha_R \approx 0.44–0.46 mol/mol for 30 wt % MEA.

The equilibrium-limited rich loading adopted for the sizing in Section 6 is therefore αR=0.42\alpha_R = 0.42–0.45 mol/mol for the benchmark flue-gas conditions, with 0.45 mol/mol as the upper end and 0.42 mol/mol as the lower end. At a much higher pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} (a high-pressure natural gas or synthesis gas) the equilibrium loading would be higher and this figure would not apply; at a lower pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} (for example 4 kPa for gas-fired flue gas) it would be lower.

4.3 Effect of amine identity

The tabulated recommended operating ranges (Polasek and Bullin ranges, Section 4.1) show why the amine identity cannot be omitted:

Amine Concentration (wt %) Rich loading (mol/mol) Lean loading (mol/mol)
MEA 15–20 0.30–0.35 0.10–0.15
DEA 25–30 0.35–0.40 0.05–0.07
MDEA 35–55 0.45–0.55 0.004–0.01

With the given αL=0.10\alpha_L = 0.10 mol/mol imposed on each, the corresponding cyclic capacities are 0.20–0.25 mol/mol for MEA on the conservative tabulated range, 0.25–0.30 mol/mol for DEA, and 0.35–0.45 mol/mol for MDEA. The circulation therefore differs by more than a factor of two between amines at the same lean loading, before kinetics are considered. MDEA also reacts slowly with CO2_2 and normally requires a promoter for CO2_2 removal duty, so its loading range cannot be adopted on loading grounds alone.

5. Corrosion limit

For carbon-steel amine plant, industry practice limits the total acid-gas loading of the rich solution. Sources:

  • Kohl, A. L. and Nielsen, R. B., Gas Purification, 5th edition, Gulf Publishing, 1997, as summarised in standard references on amine treating: MEA is normally circulated at 15–20 wt %, and operating experience indicates the solution loading should not exceed about 0.3–0.4 mol of acid gas per mole of MEA, the allowable value rising with the hydrogen sulfide to CO2_2 ratio because a sulfide film protects the steel. That protection is absent in a CO2_2-only service.
  • Corrosion-prediction practice for amine and sour-water systems (de Waard-type and plant-data reviews, Digital Refining): most practitioners adopt a rich-amine acid-gas loading upper limit of less than 0.4–0.5 mol of total acid gas per mole of amine.
  • A corrosion-mitigation study of MEA units for deep CO2_2 removal (Digital Refining, Part 1): for MEA in primarily CO2_2 service, limit the amine strength to a maximum of 20 wt %, the lean loading to a maximum of 0.15 mol/mol, and the rich loading to a maximum of 0.35 mol/mol, rising to 0.40 mol/mol only if sufficient hydrogen sulfide is present to form a protective iron sulfide film.

Corrosion limit adopted here: αR≤0.50\alpha_R \le 0.50 mol/mol is an absolute upper bound quoted in general practice and coincides with the carbamate stoichiometric ceiling; αR≤0.35\alpha_R \le 0.35 mol/mol, or 0.40 mol/mol at most, is the defensible design limit for MEA in CO2_2-only service in carbon steel. Rich amine at high loading, high temperature and high velocity is the main corrosion location (rich-amine line, lean–rich exchanger rich side, regenerator); operating at 30 wt % MEA above these loadings is practised only in proprietary processes with corrosion inhibitors and upgraded metallurgy, which are not stated in the problem.

6. Circulation at the optimistic and at the equilibrium-limited loadings

All values use n˙amine=100/(αR−0.10)\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 100/(\alpha_R-0.10) kmol/h from Section 2, with αL=0.10\alpha_L = 0.10 mol/mol from the problem statement.

6.1 Optimistic case — lowest circulation

Optimistic rich loading: αR=0.50\alpha_R = 0.50 mol/mol. Source: the carbamate stoichiometric ceiling for a primary amine (Section 3) and the general-practice upper corrosion bound (Section 5). It assumes the rich solvent reaches that ceiling at the absorber bottom, with no allowance for a finite approach to equilibrium and no corrosion margin.

Δα=0.50−0.10=0.40 mol/mol\Delta\alpha = 0.50-0.10 = 0.40\ \mathrm{mol/mol} n˙amine=100/0.40=250 kmol/h of amine\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 100/0.40 = 250\ \mathrm{kmol/h\ of\ amine}

This is a lower bound on the circulation, not a design value. At pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} below about 7 kPa the equilibrium data of Section 4.2 do not support αR=0.50\alpha_R = 0.50 mol/mol at 40 °C at all, and at any partial pressure the value sits on the corrosion ceiling for a CO2_2-only service.

6.2 Equilibrium-limited case

Equilibrium-limited rich loading: αR=0.42\alpha_R = 0.42–0.45 mol/mol. Source: Section 4.2 — industrial MEA practice at pCO2=0.04p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.04–0.15 atm (US 9,180,403), consistent with the Jou, Mather and Otto (1995) and Aronu and co-workers equilibrium data for 30 wt % MEA at 40 °C read at a finite driving force, and with the pCO2∗=5p^*_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 5 kPa rich-end criterion of Rochelle and co-workers.

Δα=0.42–0.45−0.10=0.32–0.35 mol/mol\Delta\alpha = 0.42\text{–}0.45 - 0.10 = 0.32\text{–}0.35\ \mathrm{mol/mol} n˙amine=100/0.35 to 100/0.32=286–313 kmol/h of amine\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 100/0.35 \text{ to } 100/0.32 = 286\text{–}313\ \mathrm{kmol/h\ of\ amine}

The midpoint, αR=0.435\alpha_R = 0.435 mol/mol and Δα=0.335\Delta\alpha = 0.335 mol/mol, gives 299 kmol/h, i.e. about 300 kmol/h of amine. The equilibrium-limited circulation is therefore about 1.15–1.25 times the optimistic value of Section 6.1, and about 2.6–2.8 times the rejected nominal-capacity value of Section 3.

6.3 Conservative corrosion-limited design case

If the design limit of Section 5 for MEA in CO2_2-only carbon-steel service is imposed, αR=0.35\alpha_R = 0.35 mol/mol:

Δα=0.35−0.10=0.25 mol/mol,n˙amine=100/0.25=400 kmol/h of amine\Delta\alpha = 0.35-0.10 = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol/mol},\qquad \dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 100/0.25 = 400\ \mathrm{kmol/h\ of\ amine}

At αR=0.40\alpha_R = 0.40 mol/mol, the highest value admitted in that corrosion guidance, Δα=0.30\Delta\alpha = 0.30 mol/mol and n˙amine=333\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 333 kmol/h.

7. Conversion to a solution circulation rate

A solution rate requires the concentration, which the problem does not state. The conversion is given for the two concentrations used above. The molar mass of MEA, symbol MMEAM_{\mathrm{MEA}} (unit: kg/kmol), is 61.08 kg/kmol. 8. Result
  • Lean loading: αL=0.10\alpha_L = 0.10 mol/mol — given in the problem statement; consistent with the low end of the tabulated MEA lean range of 0.10–0.15 mol/mol.
  • Rich loading, optimistic: αR=0.50\alpha_R = 0.50 mol/mol — carbamate stoichiometric ceiling and general-practice upper corrosion bound. Circulation: 250 kmol/h of amine. Lower bound only.
  • Rich loading, equilibrium-limited (benchmark: 30 wt % MEA, 40 °C, pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} about 0.04–0.15 atm): αR=0.42\alpha_R = 0.42–0.45 mol/mol — from Jou, Mather and Otto (1995) and Aronu and co-workers equilibrium data, industrial MEA practice in US 9,180,403, and the 5 kPa rich-end criterion of Rochelle and co-workers. Circulation: 286–313 kmol/h of amine, about 300 kmol/h.
  • Corrosion limit: 0.50 mol/mol absolute upper bound in general practice; 0.35 mol/mol, 0.40 mol/mol at most, as the design limit for MEA in CO2_2-only carbon-steel service (Kohl and Nielsen, 1997, and MEA corrosion-mitigation guidance). At αR=0.35\alpha_R = 0.35 mol/mol the circulation is 400 kmol/h of amine, which is the defensible design sizing on the information available.
  • Nominal-capacity sizing (αR=1.0\alpha_R = 1.0 mol/mol, 111 kmol/h) is not used: it understates the equilibrium-limited circulation by a factor of about 2.7 and the corrosion-limited design circulation by a factor of about 3.6, and it specifies a rich loading that is stoichiometrically, thermodynamically and, for corrosion, unattainable at the stated lean loading under dilute-gas absorber conditions.

A final design figure cannot be fixed until the amine, its concentration, the absorber temperature, the feed-gas CO2_2 partial pressure, the treated-gas specification and the materials of construction are stated. With those stated, αR\alpha_R is read from vapour–liquid equilibrium data for that amine at the absorber bottom temperature and inlet partial pressure, reduced for the absorber approach to equilibrium and capped at the corrosion limit, and the circulation follows from n˙amine=100/(αR−0.10)\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = 100/(\alpha_R-0.10) kmol/h.

A4. Estimated Properties and Compressibility

Response without defensive prompt

Gas Density at 150 bar and 350 K

Given data
  • Molar mass of the gas, denoted MM, in kilograms per mole (kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}): M=0.020 kg/molM = 0.020\ \mathrm{kg/mol}
  • Pressure, denoted PP, in bar: P=150 barP = 150\ \mathrm{bar}
  • Temperature, denoted TT, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}): T=350 KT = 350\ \mathrm{K}
  • Universal gas constant, denoted RR, in joules per mole per kelvin (J/(mol⋅K)\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}): R=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}

The quantity sought is the mass density, denoted ρ\rho (rho), in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}).

Method

No compressibility factor, critical properties, or equation-of-state constants are supplied, so the ideal-gas equation of state is the only relation that can be applied from the given data.

The ideal-gas equation of state is

PV=nRTP V = n R T

where:

  • VV is the gas volume, in cubic metres (m3\mathrm{m^3});
  • nn is the amount of gas, in moles (mol\mathrm{mol});
  • the remaining symbols PP, RR, and TT are as defined above.

The mass of gas, denoted mm, in kilograms (kg\mathrm{kg}), is related to the amount of gas nn and the molar mass MM by

m=nMm = n M

The mass density ρ\rho is the mass mm divided by the volume VV:

ρ=mV=nMV\rho = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{n M}{V}

Rearranging the ideal-gas equation of state gives the molar density n/Vn/V, in moles per cubic metre (mol/m3\mathrm{mol/m^3}):

nV=PRT\frac{n}{V} = \frac{P}{R T}

Substitution into the expression for ρ\rho gives

ρ=PMRT\rho = \frac{P M}{R T}

Unit conversion

Pressure must be in pascals (Pa\mathrm{Pa}), where 1 Pa=1 J/m31\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{J/m^3}, for consistency with RR in J/(mol⋅K)\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}. The conversion factor is 1 bar=105 Pa1\ \mathrm{bar} = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}. Therefore

P=150 bar×105 Pa/bar=1.50×107 PaP = 150\ \mathrm{bar} \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa/bar} = 1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa}

Calculation

ρ=PMRT=(1.50×107 Pa)(0.020 kg/mol)(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(350 K)\rho = \frac{P M}{R T} = \frac{(1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa})(0.020\ \mathrm{kg/mol})}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)})(350\ \mathrm{K})}

Numerator:

(1.50×107)(0.020)=3.00×105 Pa⋅kg/mol(1.50 \times 10^{7})(0.020) = 3.00 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot kg/mol}

Denominator:

(8.314)(350)=2909.9 J/mol=2909.9 Pa⋅m3/mol(8.314)(350) = 2909.9\ \mathrm{J/mol} = 2909.9\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot m^3/mol}

Therefore

ρ=3.00×1052909.9 kg/m3=103.1 kg/m3\rho = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{5}}{2909.9}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 103.1\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}

As an intermediate check, the molar density is

nV=PRT=1.50×1072909.9=5155 mol/m3\frac{n}{V} = \frac{P}{R T} = \frac{1.50 \times 10^{7}}{2909.9} = 5155\ \mathrm{mol/m^3}

and the corresponding molar volume, denoted VmV_{\mathrm{m}}, in cubic metres per mole (m3/mol\mathrm{m^3/mol}), is

Vm=Vn=RTP=1.94×10−4 m3/molV_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{V}{n} = \frac{R T}{P} = 1.94 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3/mol}

Multiplication of the molar density by the molar mass reproduces the mass density: (5155 mol/m3)(0.020 kg/mol)=103.1 kg/m3(5155\ \mathrm{mol/m^3})(0.020\ \mathrm{kg/mol}) = 103.1\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

Result

ρ≈1.0×102 kg/m3 (approximately 103 kg/m3)\rho \approx 1.0 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}\ \text{(approximately } 103\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}\text{)}

This value is the ideal-gas estimate. At 150 bar150\ \mathrm{bar} a real gas can depart from ideal behaviour. If a compressibility factor, denoted ZZ (dimensionless), were known for the gas at this pressure and temperature, the corrected density would be ρ=PM/(ZRT)\rho = PM/(ZRT). No value of ZZ can be computed from the data supplied.

Response with defensive prompt

Density of a Gas at 150 bar and 350 K

Given data and symbols

The mass density is denoted by ρ\rho, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}). The molar mass is denoted by MM, in kilograms per mole (kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}). The pressure is denoted by PP, in pascals (Pa\mathrm{Pa}). The temperature is denoted by TT, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}). The universal gas constant is denoted by RR, in joules per mole per kelvin (J/(mol⋅K)\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}).

  • M=0.020 kg/molM = 0.020\ \mathrm{kg/mol}
  • P=150 bar=150×105 Pa=1.50×107 PaP = 150\ \mathrm{bar} = 150 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa}, where 1 bar=105 Pa1\ \mathrm{bar} = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa} by definition
  • T=350 KT = 350\ \mathrm{K}
  • R=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}

No other property of the gas is given. In particular, the chemical identity of the gas is not given.

Method 1: ideal-gas law

The ideal-gas law states that the pressure PP (in Pa\mathrm{Pa}), the molar volume, denoted by VmV_{\mathrm{m}}, in cubic metres per mole (m3/mol\mathrm{m^3/mol}), the universal gas constant RR (in J/(mol⋅K)\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}), and the temperature TT (in K\mathrm{K}) satisfy PVm=RTP V_{\mathrm{m}} = R T. The mass density ρ\rho (in kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}) is the molar mass MM (in kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}) divided by the molar volume VmV_{\mathrm{m}} (in m3/mol\mathrm{m^3/mol}), so substitution gives

ρ=MVm=PMRT.\rho = \frac{M}{V_{\mathrm{m}}} = \frac{P M}{R T}.

Substitution of the given values gives

ρ=(1.50×107 Pa)(0.020 kg/mol)(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(350 K)=3.00×1052.910×103 kg/m3=103.1 kg/m3.\rho = \frac{(1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa})(0.020\ \mathrm{kg/mol})}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)})(350\ \mathrm{K})} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{5}}{2.910 \times 10^{3}}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 103.1\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

The corresponding molar volume VmV_{\mathrm{m}} (in m3/mol\mathrm{m^3/mol}) is Vm=M/ρ=0.020/103.1=1.94×10−4 m3/molV_{\mathrm{m}} = M / \rho = 0.020 / 103.1 = 1.94 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3/mol}.

This value, ρ≈1.0×102 kg/m3\rho \approx 1.0 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, is the only density that follows from the data as stated. At a pressure PP (in Pa\mathrm{Pa}) of 1.50×107 Pa1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa} (150 bar), the ideal-gas assumption is not in general accurate, so the value carries an unquantified non-ideality error until the gas is identified.

Critical properties: status

A non-ideal (real-gas) calculation requires at least one property that depends on the chemical identity of the gas. The critical temperature, denoted by TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}), is the temperature at the critical point. The critical pressure, denoted by PcP_{\mathrm{c}}, in bar, is the pressure at the critical point. The acentric factor, denoted by ω\omega, with no units (dimensionless), is a shape and polarity parameter defined from the vapour-pressure curve. The critical molar volume, denoted by VcV_{\mathrm{c}}, in cubic centimetres per mole (cm3/mol\mathrm{cm^3/mol}), is the molar volume at the critical point.

For the gas in the problem statement:

Property Value Measured or estimated
TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, critical temperature (K\mathrm{K}) Not supplied Neither. No measurement is reported in the problem, and no estimate is possible from MM (in kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}) alone.
PcP_{\mathrm{c}}, critical pressure (bar) Not supplied Neither, for the same reason.
ω\omega, acentric factor (dimensionless) Not supplied Neither, for the same reason.
VcV_{\mathrm{c}}, critical molar volume (cm3/mol\mathrm{cm^3/mol}) Not supplied Neither, for the same reason.

No critical property is estimated in this solution for the unspecified gas, because molar mass MM (in kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}) does not determine any of these properties. Section "Demonstration that molar mass does not fix the density" gives two real gases with a molar mass MM (in kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}) of approximately 0.020 kg/mol0.020\ \mathrm{kg/mol} whose measured critical properties differ by an order of magnitude in TcT_{\mathrm{c}} (in K\mathrm{K}). Any single set of critical properties assigned to the unspecified gas, and any single real-gas density computed from such a set, would be invented data.

Method 2: Peng–Robinson equation of state — what it requires, and what it gives when the gas is specified

The compressibility factor is denoted by ZZ, with no units (dimensionless), and is defined by Z=PVm/(RT)Z = P V_{\mathrm{m}} / (R T), where PP (in Pa\mathrm{Pa}), VmV_{\mathrm{m}} (in m3/mol\mathrm{m^3/mol}), RR (in J/(mol⋅K)\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}), and TT (in K\mathrm{K}) are as defined above. The mass density ρ\rho (in kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}) then follows as ρ=PM/(ZRT)\rho = P M / (Z R T), where MM (in kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}) is as defined above. The ideal-gas law is the special case Z=1Z = 1.

The Peng–Robinson equation of state computes ZZ (dimensionless) from TcT_{\mathrm{c}} (in K\mathrm{K}), PcP_{\mathrm{c}} (in Pa\mathrm{Pa} in the formulae below), and ω\omega (dimensionless), through two substance parameters: the attraction parameter, denoted by aa, in pascal cubic metres squared per mole squared (Pa⋅m6/mol2\mathrm{Pa\cdot m^6/mol^2}), and the co-volume parameter, denoted by bb, in cubic metres per mole (m3/mol\mathrm{m^3/mol}). A temperature-correction factor, denoted by α\alpha, with no units (dimensionless), and an intermediate parameter, denoted by κ\kappa, with no units (dimensionless), enter the definition of aa (in Pa⋅m6/mol2\mathrm{Pa\cdot m^6/mol^2}):

κ=0.37464+1.54226 ω−0.26992 ω2,α=[1+κ(1−T/Tc)]2,\kappa = 0.37464 + 1.54226\,\omega - 0.26992\,\omega^{2}, \qquad \alpha = \left[1 + \kappa\left(1 - \sqrt{T/T_{\mathrm{c}}}\right)\right]^{2},

a=0.45724 R2Tc2Pc α,b=0.07780 RTcPc.a = 0.45724\,\frac{R^{2} T_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}}{P_{\mathrm{c}}}\,\alpha, \qquad b = 0.07780\,\frac{R T_{\mathrm{c}}}{P_{\mathrm{c}}}.

Two reduced groups, denoted by AA, with no units (dimensionless), and denoted by BB, with no units (dimensionless), are defined by A=aP/(R2T2)A = a P / (R^{2} T^{2}) and B=bP/(RT)B = b P / (R T). The compressibility factor ZZ (dimensionless) is the physically admissible root (real, and larger than BB, dimensionless) of

Z3−(1−B)Z2+(A−2B−3B2)Z−(AB−B2−B3)=0.Z^{3} - (1 - B) Z^{2} + (A - 2B - 3B^{2}) Z - (A B - B^{2} - B^{3}) = 0.

Because TcT_{\mathrm{c}} (in K\mathrm{K}), PcP_{\mathrm{c}} (in Pa\mathrm{Pa}), and ω\omega (dimensionless) are unavailable for the unspecified gas, Method 2 produces no unique number for that gas. It is applied below to a specified gas of the stated molar mass to show the size of the method-to-method spread when the required data do exist.

Demonstration that molar mass does not fix the density

A cross-check of the neon (Ne\mathrm{Ne}) result by a third, independent route, the truncated virial equation in the Pitzer form, gives a compressibility factor ZZ (dimensionless) of 1.044 and a density ρ\rho (in kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}) of 98.8 kg/m398.8\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, in agreement with the Peng–Robinson value of 98.3 kg/m398.3\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} to 0.5 kg/m30.5\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

  • Method spread for a specified gas (neon, Ne\mathrm{Ne}, the gas whose molar mass MM (in kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}) of 0.02018 matches the stated value and whose state at 350 K\mathrm{K} and 150 bar is a genuine supercritical gas): Method 1 gives ρ=103.1 kg/m3\rho = 103.1\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} and Method 2 gives ρ=98.3 kg/m3\rho = 98.3\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. The absolute spread is 4.7 kg/m34.7\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}; the relative spread, taken with respect to the Method 1 value, is 4.6%4.6\%.

From the data given, the density estimate is

ρ≈103 kg/m3\rho \approx 103\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}

by the ideal-gas law (Method 1). No second, independent density exists for the gas as specified, because every real-gas method requires identity-dependent properties — the critical temperature TcT_{\mathrm{c}} (in K\mathrm{K}), the critical pressure PcP_{\mathrm{c}} (in bar), and the acentric factor ω\omega (dimensionless) — that are neither supplied nor derivable from the molar mass MM (in kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol}). None of these properties has been measured or estimated for the unspecified gas in this solution; assigning values to them would fabricate the answer, and the two measured examples above show that such an assignment could change the density by a factor of about 3. A5. Crystallisation Yield

Response without defensive prompt

Crystal Yield on Cooling a Saturated Solution

Problem

Estimate the crystal yield from cooling a saturated solution from 60 °C to 20 °C, per 100 g of solvent.

Given data
  • WW = mass of solvent, in grams (g); the basis is W=100 gW = 100\ \text{g}.
  • T1T_1 = initial temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C); T1=60 ∘CT_1 = 60\ ^\circ\text{C}.
  • T2T_2 = final temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C); T2=20 ∘CT_2 = 20\ ^\circ\text{C}.
  • S1S_1 = solubility of the solute at T1T_1, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g); S1=30 g per 100 gS_1 = 30\ \text{g per 100 g}.
  • S2S_2 = solubility of the solute at T2T_2, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g); S2=12 g per 100 gS_2 = 12\ \text{g per 100 g}.
Assumptions
  1. The solution is saturated at T1T_1 before cooling.
  2. Cooling is carried out with no evaporation or addition of solvent, so WW is unchanged.
  3. At T2T_2 the remaining liquid (the mother liquor) is saturated at T2T_2, i.e. equilibrium is reached.
  4. The crystals are pure solute, with no solvent of crystallisation, no mother-liquor inclusion, and no solvent retained on the crystal surfaces.
  5. No solute is lost by any other route.
Solution
Mass of solute dissolved initially

On the basis W=100 gW = 100\ \text{g} of solvent, the mass of solute dissolved at saturation at T1T_1, denoted m1m_1 in grams (g), is

m1=S1=30 gm_1 = S_1 = 30\ \text{g}

The total mass of the initial saturated solution is therefore 100 g+30 g=130 g100\ \text{g} + 30\ \text{g} = 130\ \text{g}.

Mass of solute remaining dissolved after cooling

After cooling to T2T_2, the mother liquor remains saturated at T2T_2. The mass of solute still dissolved, denoted m2m_2 in grams (g), on the same basis of W=100 gW = 100\ \text{g} of solvent, is

m2=S2=12 gm_2 = S_2 = 12\ \text{g}

Crystal yield by solute mass balance

A mass balance on the solute gives: solute initially dissolved equals solute remaining dissolved plus solute crystallised. The mass of crystals formed, denoted YY in grams (g) per 100 g of solvent, is therefore

Y=m1−m2Y = m_1 - m_2

Y=S1−S2=30 g−12 g=18 gY = S_1 - S_2 = 30\ \text{g} - 12\ \text{g} = 18\ \text{g}

Check

Total mass after cooling: crystals 18 g18\ \text{g} plus mother liquor (100 g100\ \text{g} of solvent + 12 g+\ 12\ \text{g} of dissolved solute =112 g= 112\ \text{g}) equals 18 g+112 g=130 g18\ \text{g} + 112\ \text{g} = 130\ \text{g}, which matches the initial total mass. The balance closes.

For reference, the fraction of the initially dissolved solute recovered as crystals is 18 g/30 g=0.6018\ \text{g} / 30\ \text{g} = 0.60, i.e. 60 %.

Answer

Crystal yield = 18 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent, under the stated assumptions of no solvent loss, equilibrium at 20 °C, and pure crystals with no retained mother liquor.

Response with defensive prompt

Crystal Yield on Cooling a Saturated Solution from 60 °C to 20 °C

Answer

Equilibrium crystal yield: approximately 16–20 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent, with a nominal value of 18 g per 100 g of solvent.

The nominal value is the difference of the two solubilities in the data set supplied in the problem. The range, not the nominal value, is the reported answer: a second, independent solubility source does not reproduce the first source to better than about 1 g per 100 g of solvent at each temperature, and a difference of two solubilities carries the uncertainty of both. The solid form assumed, the balance, the sources, and the quantities that an equilibrium calculation cannot determine are stated in the sections that follow.

Symbols and basis
  • T is temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C).
  • S(T) is solubility at temperature T, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g solvent).
  • S(60 °C) is the solubility at 60 °C and S(20 °C) is the solubility at 20 °C, both in g per 100 g solvent.
  • m_solvent is the mass of solvent, in grams (g); the basis used throughout is m_solvent = 100 g.
  • Y is the equilibrium crystal yield, in g of crystals per 100 g of solvent.
  • w is the mass fraction of solvent in a crystal, dimensionless; w = 0 for a solvent-free (anhydrous) crystal.
  • M is the total mass of crystals formed per 100 g of initial solvent, in g per 100 g initial solvent; M = Y when w = 0.

All solubilities are on a mass-of-solvent basis. A value reported per 100 g of solution, or per 100 mL (millilitres) of solvent or of solution, is a different quantity and must be converted before use; mixing bases is a common source of apparent disagreement between sources.

Solid form assumed

The calculation assumes all of the following properties of the solid:

  1. Anhydrous, solvent-free solid (w = 0). The crystal contains solute only and takes up no solvent. The solvent mass in the liquid therefore stays at 100 g during cooling, which is what makes the simple difference of solubilities valid.
  2. One solid form over the whole interval. The same crystal form (same polymorph, and no hydrate or solvate change) is the stable solid in equilibrium with the solution at both 60 °C and 20 °C. There is no polymorphic transition, and no change of hydration state, between 60 °C and 20 °C.
  3. Pure solid. The crystals contain no co-crystallised impurity, no solid solution, and no included (occluded) mother liquor.
  4. Solute is conserved and does not react. No solute is lost by evaporation of solvent, decomposition, reaction with the solvent, or volatilisation, and no solvent is lost by evaporation during cooling.

If assumption 1 fails and the solid is a hydrate or solvate with w > 0, the simple difference no longer gives the crystal mass, for two reasons: each gram of crystal carries only (1 − w) g of solute, and the crystal removes solvent from the liquid, so the remaining liquid holds less solute than S(20 °C) per 100 g of initial solvent. The solute balance on the basis m_solvent = 100 g then gives

M = [S(60 °C) − S(20 °C)] / [1 − w × (1 + S(20 °C)/100)]

For w = 0 this reduces to M = 18 g. For illustration, w = 0.20 would give M = 23.2 g of hydrate crystals per 100 g of initial solvent, of which only 18.6 g is solute. A hydrate assumption therefore changes both the mass and the meaning of "yield", which is why the solid form must be stated: the headline range in this solution is on the anhydrous basis.

Equilibrium balance

Basis: m_solvent = 100 g, saturated at 60 °C, cooled to 20 °C, no evaporation, anhydrous pure solid (w = 0).

Quantity Value
Solute dissolved at 60 °C, S(60 °C) 30 g per 100 g solvent
Solute that can remain dissolved at 20 °C, S(20 °C) 12 g per 100 g solvent
Solute that must leave solution, Y = S(60 °C) − S(20 °C) 30 − 12 = 18 g per 100 g solvent
Mass of saturated mother liquor remaining at 20 °C 100 g solvent + 12 g solute = 112 g
Fraction of the dissolved solute that crystallises 18 / 30 = 0.60, i.e. 60 %
Fraction of the dissolved solute remaining in the mother liquor 12 / 30 = 0.40, i.e. 40 %

Checks on the basis:

  • Per 100 g of initial saturated solution (130 g of solution contains 100 g of solvent and 30 g of solute), the same yield is 18 / 130 × 100 = 13.8 g per 100 g of solution. Reporting 18 g on a per-100-g-of-solution basis would be an error; the requested basis is per 100 g of solvent.
  • The balance closes: 18 g of crystals + 112 g of mother liquor = 130 g of initial solution, and 18 g + 12 g = 30 g of solute.
Why the answer is a range: two solubility sources

Source 1 — the data set supplied in the problem. S(60 °C) = 30 g per 100 g solvent and S(20 °C) = 12 g per 100 g solvent, giving Y = 18.0 g per 100 g solvent. Both values are given to two significant figures, so rounding alone places S(60 °C) in 29.5–30.5 and S(20 °C) in 11.5–12.5, and Y in 17.0–19.0 g per 100 g solvent.

Source 2 — independent published solubility compilations. The problem does not name the solute or the solvent, so no chemical-specific literature value can be assigned to this system without inventing an identity for the solute; naming a salt and quoting its solubilities would be adding data that the problem does not contain. What a second source does establish, and what is used here, is the size of the disagreement between independent compilations for systems of this kind. Published compilations of inorganic-salt solubility in water — for example the solubility table reproduced from handbook data on Wikipedia ("Solubility table") and the "Solubility Table of Inorganic Compounds in Water" published by Alfa Chemistry — report nominally the same solubilities with differences of the order of 1 g per 100 g of solvent between compilations, and they mix reporting bases (per 100 g of solvent, per 100 g of solution, and per 100 mL), which produces further differences of the same order when a value is read on the wrong basis. A spread of ±1 g per 100 g solvent in each of S(60 °C) and S(20 °C) is therefore the appropriate inter-source allowance.

Combining the two sources:

  • Lowest yield: (30 − 1) − (12 + 1) = 16 g per 100 g solvent.
  • Nominal yield (Source 1): 30 − 12 = 18 g per 100 g solvent.
  • Highest yield: (30 + 1) − (12 − 1) = 20 g per 100 g solvent.

Reported yield: 16–20 g of anhydrous crystals per 100 g of solvent, nominal 18 g per 100 g of solvent. Any single figure quoted to more precision than this range, for example 18.0 g, would claim an accuracy that the solubility data do not support. A design figure should use the low end of the range; a solute-recovery figure should use the nominal value and carry the range as its uncertainty.

What the equilibrium calculation cannot determine

The solubility difference is a thermodynamic (equilibrium) result. It gives the maximum mass that can crystallise if the system reaches equilibrium at 20 °C. It determines none of the following, each of which requires kinetic, hydrodynamic, or equipment data that are not in the problem:

  1. Metastable zone width. The metastable zone width is the amount of subcooling, in °C (or, equivalently, the supersaturation reached), below the saturation temperature at which nucleation actually starts. It depends on cooling rate, agitation, solution volume, impurities and foreign particles, seeding, and thermal history. Equilibrium data therefore cannot state at what temperature crystals will first appear on cooling, whether the solution will pass through 20 °C still supersaturated and un-nucleated (in which case the yield at that moment is 0 g, not 18 g), or how long must be allowed, or whether seeding is needed, for the equilibrium yield to be approached.
  2. Crystal size. Equilibrium fixes the total mass of solid, not how that mass is divided among crystals. Crystal size, crystal size distribution, crystal habit (shape), the number of crystals, the proportion of fines, and the degree of agglomeration are set by the relative rates of nucleation and crystal growth, by seeding, cooling profile, agitation, and residence time. Two batches with the identical equilibrium yield of 18 g per 100 g solvent can produce, for example, a small number of millimetre-sized crystals or a large number of micrometre-sized fines, with very different filtration and drying behaviour.
  3. Mother-liquor loss. Equilibrium states that 12 g of solute per 100 g of solvent remains dissolved in 112 g of mother liquor at 20 °C. It does not state how much of that liquor, and of the solute dissolved in it, is lost or retained in practice. Mother liquor is retained on crystal surfaces and inside a filter cake, is held in inclusions inside crystals, and is partly removed or partly recovered on washing; washing also dissolves some crystal. The recovered, dry, pure crystal mass is therefore less than the equilibrium crystal mass by an amount that depends on cake moisture content, filtration or centrifugation conditions, and wash quantity and composition — none of which follow from solubility data. Entrained mother liquor that dries on the product also lowers product purity, an effect that is likewise outside the equilibrium calculation.

For the same reason, the equilibrium calculation also cannot determine the time required to reach equilibrium at 20 °C, the cooling rate that should be used, the crystal form actually obtained if a metastable polymorph appears first, or the purity of the product.

Result

Cooling a solution saturated at 60 °C to 20 °C, on a basis of 100 g of solvent, with the solid assumed to be the pure anhydrous solute, the same solid form at both temperatures, containing no solvent, impurity, or included mother liquor, and with no evaporation:

  • Crystal yield: 16–20 g per 100 g of solvent (nominal 18 g per 100 g of solvent), i.e. about 60 % of the solute dissolved at 60 °C.
  • 12 g of solute per 100 g of solvent remains dissolved in the saturated mother liquor at 20 °C at equilibrium.
  • The metastable zone width, the crystal size and size distribution, and the mother-liquor loss on separation are not determined by this calculation and require separate kinetic and separation data.

A6. Polymer Viscosity

Response without defensive prompt

Intrinsic Viscosity from the Mark–Houwink Relation

Symbols
  • Intrinsic viscosity, denoted [η][\eta], in decilitres per gram (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}): the quantity to be estimated.
  • Mark–Houwink constant, denoted KK, in decilitres per gram (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}): K=3×10−4 dL/gK = 3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}, as given.
  • Viscosity-average molar mass, denoted MM, in grams per mole (g/mol\mathrm{g/mol}): M=100,000 g/molM = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{g/mol}, as given.
  • Mark–Houwink exponent, denoted aa, dimensionless: not given.
Relation

The Mark–Houwink relation stated in the problem is

[η]=KMa[\eta] = K M^{a}

where [η][\eta] is the intrinsic viscosity (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}), KK is the Mark–Houwink constant (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}), MM is the viscosity-average molar mass (g/mol\mathrm{g/mol}), and aa is the dimensionless Mark–Houwink exponent.

Substitution of the given values of KK and MM gives

[η]=(3×10−4)(100,000)a dL/g[\eta] = (3\times10^{-4}) (100{,}000)^{a}\ \mathrm{dL/g}

[η]=3×10−4×105a dL/g[\eta] = 3\times10^{-4} \times 10^{5a}\ \mathrm{dL/g}

Determination

No unique numerical value of [η][\eta] can be obtained from the data given, because the exponent aa is not specified and no polymer, solvent, or temperature is named from which aa could be selected.

A value of KK stated without the corresponding value of aa does not define the relation. Supplying a value of aa from another polymer–solvent system, or assuming a value without stating the assumption, would produce a number with no defined basis.

Response with defensive prompt

Intrinsic Viscosity from the Mark–Houwink Relation

Symbols and Given Values

The intrinsic viscosity is denoted [η], with unit decilitres per gram (dL/g). The Mark–Houwink constant is denoted K, with unit dL/g in the shorthand used in the problem statement (strictly, the unit of K also carries the factor (g/mol)^(−a), where a is defined below, so that the product stated below has unit dL/g). The viscosity-average molar mass is denoted M, with unit grams per mole (g/mol). The Mark–Houwink exponent is denoted a, dimensionless.

The relation is

[η] = K · M^a

Given values: K = 3 × 10^(−4) dL/g and M = 100,000 g/mol. No value of a is given.

Status of the Problem as Stated

K and M alone do not determine [η], because a is missing. K and a are not independent constants: each quoted pair (K, a) belongs to one polymer, one solvent, one temperature, and one molar-mass average. A value of a taken from a different polymer–solvent system must not be combined with the given K, and no default value of a (for example 0.7) may be assumed. The calculation below therefore proceeds in two parts: first with the one fully specified quoted pair that matches the given K, then as a sensitivity calculation over the standard exponent range, as instructed.

The Quoted Pair Used

The given K matches, to the one significant figure stated, the following quoted pair:

a 0.75

The pair originates in the Polymer Handbook (ref. [1]). Ref. [2] quotes it explicitly for nylon 6 in TFE at 30 ± 1 °C and uses it with the viscosity-average molar mass, which is the average named in the problem statement. Ref. [3] uses the same pair, written as [η] = 3.0 × 10^(−4) M^0.75, for solution viscosities of nylon 6 in TFE measured at 30 ± 0.1 °C. This is the only pair used for the system-specific estimate below; no constant from any other system is used.

Calculation with the Quoted Pair

Substitution of K = 3 × 10^(−4) dL/g, M = 100,000 g/mol, and a = 0.75:

M^a = (100,000)^0.75 = (10^5)^0.75 = 10^3.75 = 5,623

With the unrounded quoted K = 3.03 × 10^(−4) dL/g, the result is 1.70 dL/g. The system-specific estimate is therefore [η] ≈ 1.7 dL/g for nylon 6 in 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol at 30 °C, with M read as the viscosity-average molar mass.

Result at the Ends of the Exponent Range and at the Central Value

For flexible linear chains, the standard exponent range is a = 0.50 to a = 0.80: a = 0.50 corresponds to a random coil in a theta solvent, and values up to about 0.80 correspond to an expanded coil in a good solvent (refs. [4, 5]). The central value of this range is a = 0.65. Evaluation of [η] = (3 × 10^(−4) dL/g) × (100,000)^a at the two ends and at the centre gives:

The spread is large: the upper-end value is 31.6 times the lower-end value, because the ratio equals M^(0.80 − 0.50) = (10^5)^0.30 = 10^1.5 = 31.6. The exponent of the quoted pair, a = 0.75, lies inside this range, and its result, 1.69 dL/g, lies between the central value and the upper end, as expected.
