Response with defensive prompt

Actual Tray Count from Theoretical Stages

Given quantities
  • NthN_{\mathrm{th}} is the number of theoretical (equilibrium) stages required for the separation, dimensionless as a count. Here Nth=20N_{\mathrm{th}} = 20.
  • EoE_{\mathrm{o}} is the overall column efficiency, dimensionless. Here Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65.
  • NaN_{\mathrm{a}} is the number of actual trays required, dimensionless as a count. NaN_{\mathrm{a}} is to be found.
Type of efficiency

EoE_{\mathrm{o}} is an overall column efficiency, not a Murphree efficiency.

  • Overall column efficiency applies to the column as a whole. It is defined as the number of theoretical stages divided by the number of actual trays that achieve the same separation.
  • Murphree efficiency applies to a single tray. It is defined for one tray as the actual change in vapour composition across that tray divided by the change that would occur if the vapour leaving the tray were in equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray. A Murphree efficiency is therefore a per-tray quantity, it can vary from tray to tray, and it is not in general equal to EoE_{\mathrm{o}}. A Murphree value cannot be inserted directly into the overall stage-to-tray conversion below without a further relation that accounts for the liquid and vapour flow pattern in the column.
Correlation

The standard empirical correlation for an overall column efficiency of this kind is the O'Connell correlation (O'Connell, 1946).

In that correlation, αa\alpha_{\mathrm{a}} is the average relative volatility of the light key component relative to the heavy key component, dimensionless, and μa\mu_{\mathrm{a}} is the molar average liquid viscosity of the feed, in millinewton second per square metre (mN s m−2\mathrm{mN\,s\,m^{-2}}, numerically equal to millipascal second, mPa s\mathrm{mPa\,s}), each evaluated at the average column temperature. The correlation relates EoE_{\mathrm{o}} to the product μaαa\mu_{\mathrm{a}}\alpha_{\mathrm{a}}. The form fitted by Eduljee (1958) to the O'Connell plot, with EoE_{\mathrm{o}} expressed as a percentage and log⁡\log denoting the logarithm to base 10, is:

Eo  (%)=51−32.5log⁡(μaαa)E_{\mathrm{o}}\;(\%) = 51 - 32.5 \log(\mu_{\mathrm{a}}\alpha_{\mathrm{a}})

Fitted systems: the correlation was based mainly on data from hydrocarbon systems, with some values for chlorinated solvents and for water–alcohol mixtures, obtained on commercial columns fitted predominantly with bubble-cap trays. It gives reliable estimates for hydrocarbon systems and approximate estimates for other systems. It uses only the two physical-property variables αa\alpha_{\mathrm{a}} and μa\mu_{\mathrm{a}} and takes no account of tray design parameters.

No values of αa\alpha_{\mathrm{a}} and μa\mu_{\mathrm{a}} are supplied in this problem, so EoE_{\mathrm{o}} cannot be re-estimated from the O'Connell correlation here and does not need to be: the value Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 is given and is used directly.

Calculation

By the definition of overall column efficiency stated above:

Eo=NthNaE_{\mathrm{o}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{th}}}{N_{\mathrm{a}}}

Rearranging for NaN_{\mathrm{a}}:

Na=NthEo=200.65=30.77N_{\mathrm{a}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{th}}}{E_{\mathrm{o}}} = \frac{20}{0.65} = 30.77

A fractional tray cannot be installed, and rounding down would provide fewer trays than the separation requires, so the result is rounded up to the next whole tray:

Na=31 actual traysN_{\mathrm{a}} = 31 \text{ actual trays}

This count is the number of actual trays corresponding to the 20 theoretical stages under the stage-counting convention in the statement of the problem. A reboiler is separate equipment and is not itself a tray; if a stage count from another source includes a reboiler stage, that stage must be removed from the count before the conversion is applied to trays alone.

Sensitivity to the efficiency value

The same conversion, Na=Nth/EoN_{\mathrm{a}} = N_{\mathrm{th}} / E_{\mathrm{o}} with Nth=20N_{\mathrm{th}} = 20, with rounding up to a whole number of trays in each case:

EoE_{\mathrm{o}}, dimensionless Na=20/EoN_{\mathrm{a}} = 20 / E_{\mathrm{o}}, trays Actual trays installed
0.40 50.00 50
0.65 30.77 31
0.90 22.22 23

A lower overall efficiency requires more actual trays for the same 20 theoretical stages, and a higher overall efficiency requires fewer.

Result

20 theoretical stages at an overall column efficiency Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 require 31 actual trays. At Eo=0.40E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.40 the requirement is 50 actual trays, and at Eo=0.90E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.90 the requirement is 23 actual trays.

References
  • O'Connell, H. E. (1946). Plate efficiency of fractionating columns and absorbers. Transactions of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers, 42, 741.
  • Eduljee, H. E. (1958) — equation form of the O'Connell correlation, as cited in Coulson and Richardson (below).
  • Coulson, J. M., and Richardson, J. F. Chemical Engineering, Volume 2 — statement of the O'Connell correlation, its fitted systems (mainly hydrocarbons, with some chlorinated solvents and water–alcohol mixtures), and its scope.

No numerical fouled area can be given from the statement as supplied, for the following reason. The instruction refers to "the tabulated fouling resistance for the named service", but no service is named in the problem, and no table, source, or numerical value of RfR_{\mathrm{f}} is given. Fouling resistance depends on the fluids and the service — for example, cooling water, crude oil, steam and a clean solvent carry different tabulated values in standard tables, and values also differ between tables and between a resistance quoted for one side and a total resistance for both sides. Selecting a service or a table value that was not supplied would invent the deciding input. The two results that a completed statement would produce are therefore left in the closed forms above:

Cleaning interval

No cleaning interval is implied by the area, and none can be stated from the supplied data.

A tabulated fouling resistance is a design allowance: a value of resistance that the exchanger is sized to tolerate. It is not a rate. An interval requires a relation between fouling resistance and time. The time from cleaning is denoted by the symbol tt, in hours (h) or months, as applicable. A cleaning interval would follow only from a stated growth relation for RfR_{\mathrm{f}} as a function of tt, together with the limiting value of RfR_{\mathrm{f}} at which cleaning is required, or equivalently a stated fouling rate; for a linear growth relation, the interval would be the limiting resistance divided by that rate. Neither a growth relation, a fouling rate, an operating schedule, nor a limiting resistance tied to time is given.

Sizing the exchanger to the tabulated resistance therefore states only that the duty of 2 MW at a logarithmic mean temperature difference of 20 K is still met when the fouling resistance has reached that allowance. It does not state when that resistance is reached. Any interval in months or years would require data not in the problem.

Result

No unique numerical pressure drop can be estimated from the data given. The single supplied value fixes only the liquid-only reference pressure drop. The two-phase pressure drop is that reference value multiplied by a two-phase multiplier, and the multiplier cannot be obtained without, at minimum, the relative flow rates and the physical properties of the two phases.

Any single number stated without those additional data would rest on values invented for the missing quantities. The determinate result, the data needed to complete the estimate, and the size of the resulting uncertainty are given below.

Symbols
  • ΔPtp\Delta P_{\mathrm{tp}} is the frictional pressure drop of the actual gas–liquid (two-phase) mixture over the line length considered, in bar.
  • ΔPLO\Delta P_{\mathrm{LO}} is the liquid-only pressure drop, computed as if the total mass flow rate flowed as liquid alone in the same pipe, in bar. The given value is ΔPLO=0.4 bar\Delta P_{\mathrm{LO}} = 0.4\ \mathrm{bar} over a length of 1 km1\ \mathrm{km}.
  • ϕLO2\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} is the dimensionless two-phase multiplier referred to the liquid-only pressure drop, defined by the ratio in Eq. (1).
  • ΔPL\Delta P_{\mathrm{L}} is the pressure drop that the liquid phase alone would give if it flowed alone in the pipe at its own mass flow rate (not the total mass flow rate), in bar.
  • ΔPG\Delta P_{\mathrm{G}} is the pressure drop that the gas phase alone would give if it flowed alone in the pipe at its own mass flow rate, in bar.
  • XX is the dimensionless Lockhart–Martinelli parameter, defined in Eq. (3).
  • CC is the dimensionless Chisholm constant, whose value depends on whether each phase, flowing alone, would be laminar or turbulent.
Governing relation

The standard route from a liquid-only value to a two-phase value is the Lockhart–Martinelli correlation, in the algebraic form given by Chisholm:

ϕLO2=ΔPtpΔPLO(1)\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} = \frac{\Delta P_{\mathrm{tp}}}{\Delta P_{\mathrm{LO}}} \tag{1}

ϕLO2=1+CX+1X2(2)\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} = 1 + \frac{C}{X} + \frac{1}{X^{2}} \tag{2}

X2=ΔPLΔPG(3)X^{2} = \frac{\Delta P_{\mathrm{L}}}{\Delta P_{\mathrm{G}}} \tag{3}

Combination of Eqs. (1) and (2) with the given value gives

ΔPtp=0.4(1+CX+1X2) bar per km.(4)\Delta P_{\mathrm{tp}} = 0.4\left(1 + \frac{C}{X} + \frac{1}{X^{2}}\right)\ \mathrm{bar\ per\ km}. \tag{4}

Equation (4) is as far as the supplied data go. Neither XX nor CC is given, and neither can be recovered from ΔPLO\Delta P_{\mathrm{LO}} alone.

Note the distinction that the problem statement makes necessary: ΔPLO\Delta P_{\mathrm{LO}} (total flow as liquid) is not ΔPL\Delta P_{\mathrm{L}} (liquid phase only, at its own rate). Confusing the two does not supply XX; it only sets XX to a wrong value.

Why the missing quantities matter

The parameter XX measures the relative frictional resistance of the two phases flowing separately. A gas-rich mixture has a small XX and a large multiplier; a liquid-rich mixture has a large XX and a multiplier near unity. The constant CC takes the values 5, 10, 12, or 20 in the Chisholm form, according to the combination of laminar and turbulent flow of the liquid and gas phases flowing alone, with C=20C = 20 for both phases turbulent.

Values of Eq. (4) over a plausible range of XX and the full range of CC are:

XX (–) ΔPtp\Delta P_{\mathrm{tp}} at C=5C = 5 (bar per km) ΔPtp\Delta P_{\mathrm{tp}} at C=20C = 20 (bar per km)
0.1 60.4 120.4
0.5 6.0 18.0
1 2.8 8.8
2 1.5 4.5
5 0.82 2.02
10 0.60 1.20

These values are an illustration of sensitivity, not an estimate. Across this range alone the answer varies by a factor of about 200, from a value close to the liquid-only value to more than 100 bar per km100\ \mathrm{bar\ per\ km}. No narrower range can be defended without information about the mixture.

Two further points do not remove the indeterminacy:

  1. Elevation. The line is horizontal, so there is no static head contribution from a change in elevation. This removes one term of the total pressure drop; it says nothing about the frictional term, which is the term the multiplier corrects.
  2. Acceleration. A change in mixture density along the line, for example from gas expansion as pressure falls or from flashing, gives an additional accelerational pressure change. Evaluating it requires inlet and outlet phase fractions and densities, which are also not given. For a modest frictional drop in a line at high pressure this term is often small, but that condition has not been stated and cannot be assumed here.

One bound does follow from Eq. (2): for positive CC and XX, ϕLO2>1\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} > 1, so the two-phase frictional pressure drop exceeds 0.4 bar per km0.4\ \mathrm{bar\ per\ km}. That inequality is the only numerical conclusion the data support.

Data required for a numerical estimate

A completed estimate requires, as a minimum:

  1. The mass flow rate of each phase separately, or equivalently the total mass flow rate and the mass fraction of gas in the mixture, so that ΔPL\Delta P_{\mathrm{L}} and ΔPG\Delta P_{\mathrm{G}}, and hence XX, can be computed.
  2. The density and the viscosity of the liquid, and the density and the viscosity of the gas at line conditions (pressure and temperature), which enter ΔPL\Delta P_{\mathrm{L}} and ΔPG\Delta P_{\mathrm{G}} and decide whether each phase is laminar or turbulent, and hence the value of CC.
  3. The pipe internal diameter and roughness, unless ΔPL\Delta P_{\mathrm{L}} and ΔPG\Delta P_{\mathrm{G}} are supplied directly; these are needed to compute the two single-phase pressure drops from the phase flow rates.
  4. A statement of the flow pattern or of conditions sufficient to select a correlation, since the Lockhart–Martinelli form is one of several two-phase correlations and its accuracy depends on the flow pattern.

With items 1–3, XX and CC follow, Eq. (4) gives a single value, and the result can be checked against a second correlation, for example a homogeneous-flow calculation or the Friedel correlation, to give an uncertainty range.

Conclusion

ΔPtp=0.4 ϕLO2 bar per km,ϕLO2=1+CX+1X2,ΔPtp>0.4 bar per km\Delta P_{\mathrm{tp}} = 0.4\,\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}\ \mathrm{bar\ per\ km}, \qquad \phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} = 1 + \frac{C}{X} + \frac{1}{X^{2}}, \qquad \Delta P_{\mathrm{tp}} > 0.4\ \mathrm{bar\ per\ km}

The problem as stated is underdetermined: the liquid-only pressure drop of 0.4 bar per km0.4\ \mathrm{bar\ per\ km} supplies the reference value only, and the phase split and phase properties needed for the two-phase multiplier are absent. A numerical estimate requires the additional data listed above.

Response with defensive prompt

Gas–liquid pressure drop over 1 km of horizontal line

Conclusion

No unique pressure drop, flow regime, or liquid hold-up can be obtained from the data supplied. The single datum supplied fixes only a reference single-phase gradient. Every two-phase quantity requested depends on further quantities that are not given, and plausible values of those quantities change the result by more than an order of magnitude. The sections below define the quantities involved, show the calculation that each named method requires, state exactly which inputs are missing, and give conditional numerical illustrations — labelled as illustrations, not as results for this line — to quantify the sensitivity.

1. Given datum and symbols

Symbols are defined at first use, with SI units where applicable.

  • LL is the line length, in metres (m): L=1000 mL = 1000\ \mathrm{m} (1 km).
  • (dp/dz)lo(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{lo} is the liquid-only pressure gradient, in pascal per metre (Pa m−1^{-1}), computed as if the total mass flow were liquid alone. The supplied value is 0.4 bar km−10.4\ \mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}, i.e. 0.4 bar0.4\ \mathrm{bar} over LL, or 40 Pa m−140\ \mathrm{Pa\ m^{-1}}.
  • (dp/dz)TP(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{TP} is the actual two-phase frictional pressure gradient, in Pa m−1^{-1}. For a horizontal line there is no elevation (hydrostatic) term; an acceleration (momentum-change) term can still arise if the gas expands as pressure falls, and it also cannot be evaluated from the datum supplied (see §5).
  • ΔpTP\Delta p_{TP} is the two-phase pressure drop over LL, in pascal (Pa) or bar: ΔpTP=(dp/dz)TPL\Delta p_{TP} = (\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{TP} L when the gradient is treated as constant over LL.

The two-phase multiplier based on the liquid-only gradient is

Φlo2=(dp/dz)TP(dp/dz)lo,ΔpTP=0.4 Φlo2 bar per km.\Phi_{lo}^{2} = \frac{(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{TP}}{(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{lo}}, \qquad \Delta p_{TP} = 0.4\,\Phi_{lo}^{2}\ \mathrm{bar\ per\ km}.

Hence the whole problem reduces to finding Φlo2\Phi_{lo}^{2}. That multiplier is not a constant of the line; it is a function of the composition and properties of the mixture, which are not supplied.

2. Quantities required and not supplied
  • xx is the gas mass fraction (quality), dimensionless: the gas mass flow rate, in kilogram per second (kg s−1^{-1}), divided by the total mass flow rate, in kg s−1^{-1}. Not given.
  • ρL\rho_L is the liquid density, in kilogram per cubic metre (kg m−3^{-3}), and ρG\rho_G is the gas density, in kg m−3^{-3}, at line temperature and pressure. Neither is given; even their ratio ρL/ρG\rho_L/\rho_G is not given.
  • μL\mu_L is the liquid dynamic viscosity, in pascal second (Pa s), and μG\mu_G is the gas dynamic viscosity, in Pa s. Not given.
  • DD is the internal pipe diameter, in m. Not given.
  • jLj_L is the liquid superficial velocity, in metre per second (m s−1^{-1}): the liquid volumetric flow rate, in cubic metre per second (m3^{3} s−1^{-1}), divided by the pipe cross-sectional area, in square metre (m2^{2}). jGj_G is the corresponding gas superficial velocity, in m s−1^{-1}. Neither is given, and neither can be recovered from (dp/dz)lo(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{lo} without DD, the total mass flux and the fluid properties.
  • σ\sigma is the gas–liquid surface tension, in newton per metre (N m−1^{-1}). Not given; it enters regime criteria for stratified and annular flow.

Without at least xx, ρL/ρG\rho_L/\rho_G, μL\mu_L and μG\mu_G, and, for a regime prediction, jLj_L, jGj_G and DD, no named correlation can be evaluated.

3. Flow regime: not predictable from the datum

Flow-regime maps and transition criteria — for example the Baker map, the Mandhane map, and the Taitel–Dukler criteria — are constructed in coordinates formed from jLj_L and jGj_G (or equivalent mass fluxes), corrected in some maps by ρL\rho_L, ρG\rho_G, μL\mu_L and σ\sigma. Horizontal flow can be bubble, plug, slug (intermittent), stratified smooth, stratified wavy, or annular, depending on those coordinates.

The supplied datum is one scalar, 0.4 bar km−10.4\ \mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}. The same liquid-only gradient is compatible with, for example:

  • a small jGj_G and a moderate jLj_L, giving bubble or plug flow;
  • comparable jGj_G and jLj_L at intermediate rates, giving slug flow, with its unsteady pressure fluctuations; and
  • a large jGj_G and a small jLj_L, giving annular flow.

No coordinate on any regime map can be placed, so no regime — and no regime-dependent choice of correlation constant (see §4.2) — is justified. Assigning a regime from the datum alone would be invention.

4. Pressure drop by the two named methods
4.1 Homogeneous method

The homogeneous model treats the mixture as a single pseudo-fluid flowing with no slip between the phases.

  • ρH\rho_H is the homogeneous mixture density, in kg m−3^{-3}, defined by 1/ρH=x/ρG+(1−x)/ρL1/\rho_H = x/\rho_G + (1-x)/\rho_L.
  • μH\mu_H is a homogeneous mixture viscosity, in Pa s; one common definition (McAdams form) is 1/μH=x/μG+(1−x)/μL1/\mu_H = x/\mu_G + (1-x)/\mu_L.
  • Φlo,H2\Phi_{lo,H}^{2} is the homogeneous value of the multiplier defined in §1. With a Blasius-type friction law it is, to the usual approximation,

Φlo,H2≈ρLρH(μHμL)0.25=[(1−x)+x ρLρG](μHμL)0.25.\Phi_{lo,H}^{2} \approx \frac{\rho_L}{\rho_H}\left(\frac{\mu_H}{\mu_L}\right)^{0.25} = \left[(1-x) + x\,\frac{\rho_L}{\rho_G}\right]\left(\frac{\mu_H}{\mu_L}\right)^{0.25}.

Even setting the viscosity factor to unity leaves Φlo,H2≈(1−x)+x ρL/ρG\Phi_{lo,H}^{2} \approx (1-x) + x\,\rho_L/\rho_G, which requires both xx and ρL/ρG\rho_L/\rho_G — neither supplied.

Hold-up implied by the homogeneous method:

  • α\alpha is the gas void fraction, dimensionless: gas volume divided by total volume in a line section.
  • HLH_L is the liquid hold-up, dimensionless: HL=1−αH_L = 1 - \alpha.

No slip means each phase travels at the mixture velocity, so the in-situ volume fractions equal the flowing volume fractions:

αH=x/ρGx/ρG+(1−x)/ρL,HL,H=1−x(1−x)+x ρL/ρG.\alpha_H = \frac{x/\rho_G}{x/\rho_G + (1-x)/\rho_L}, \qquad H_{L,H} = \frac{1-x}{(1-x) + x\,\rho_L/\rho_G}.

Both require xx and ρL/ρG\rho_L/\rho_G.

4.2 Separated-flow method: Lockhart–Martinelli

The separated model treats each phase as flowing alone in the pipe, with interaction represented by an empirical multiplier.

  • (dp/dz)L(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_L is the pressure gradient, in Pa m−1^{-1}, that the liquid phase alone would produce flowing at its own rate in the pipe. (dp/dz)G(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_G is the corresponding gas-only gradient, in Pa m−1^{-1}.
  • XX is the Lockhart–Martinelli parameter, dimensionless, defined by X2=(dp/dz)L / (dp/dz)GX^{2} = (\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_L\,/\,(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_G.
  • ΦL2\Phi_L^{2} is the multiplier on the liquid-phase gradient, defined by (dp/dz)TP=ΦL2 (dp/dz)L(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{TP} = \Phi_L^{2}\,(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_L, with the standard correlation ΦL2=1+C/X+1/X2\Phi_L^{2} = 1 + C/X + 1/X^{2}.
  • CC is the Lockhart–Martinelli interaction constant, dimensionless: C=20C = 20 for turbulent liquid–turbulent gas, 1212 for viscous liquid–turbulent gas, 1010 for turbulent liquid–viscous gas, and 55 for viscous liquid–viscous gas. Selecting CC requires the Reynolds number of each phase, hence μL\mu_L, μG\mu_G, DD and the phase rates.

Note the distinction that makes the supplied datum insufficient here: (dp/dz)lo(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{lo} corresponds to the total flow as liquid, whereas the correlation needs (dp/dz)L(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_L for the liquid part only at its own (lower) rate, and (dp/dz)G(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_G for the gas part. Neither follows from (dp/dz)lo(\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{lo} without xx and the friction law exponents for each phase. XX is therefore unknown, and ΦL2\Phi_L^{2} varies steeply with XX: with C=20C = 20, ΦL2=301\Phi_L^{2} = 301 at X=0.1X = 0.1, 2222 at X=1X = 1, and 3.013.01 at X=10X = 10.

Hold-up implied by the separated method:

  • SS is the slip ratio, dimensionless: S=uG/uLS = u_G/u_L, where uGu_G is the in-situ gas velocity, in m s−1^{-1}, and uLu_L is the in-situ liquid velocity, in m s−1^{-1}. The separated model has S>1S > 1: the gas travels faster, so liquid accumulates in the line relative to the flowing proportions.

α=11+S 1−xx ρGρL,HL=1−α.\alpha = \frac{1}{1 + S\,\dfrac{1-x}{x}\,\dfrac{\rho_G}{\rho_L}}, \qquad H_L = 1 - \alpha.

For the same xx and ρL/ρG\rho_L/\rho_G, HLH_L in the separated model is therefore larger than HL,HH_{L,H} of §4.1, by an amount set by SS. SS is not supplied and is not given by the Lockhart–Martinelli friction correlation itself; it requires a separate hold-up relation (for example the Zivi minimum-entropy-production estimate S=(ρL/ρG)1/3S = (\rho_L/\rho_G)^{1/3}, or an empirical Lockhart–Martinelli hold-up correlation). No separated-flow hold-up number follows from the datum supplied.

5. Further term that cannot be checked

If the pressure falls appreciably along LL, the gas expands, xx stays fixed on a mass basis but jGj_G and ρG\rho_G change, and an acceleration pressure gradient adds to the frictional gradient. Whether that term is negligible depends on the absolute pressure level and on ρG\rho_G, neither of which is given. Any single-gradient estimate implicitly assumes constant properties along the kilometre; that assumption cannot be verified here.

7. Data that would make the problem determinate

A defensible estimate requires, at minimum:

  1. xx, or the separate gas and liquid mass (or volumetric) flow rates;
  2. ρL\rho_L and ρG\rho_G at line conditions, i.e. the fluids' identity (or their densities), the line pressure, and the line temperature;
  3. μL\mu_L and μG\mu_G at line conditions;
  4. DD (and, for a refined frictional calculation, the pipe roughness);
  5. the inlet pressure, so that gas expansion and the acceleration term along the kilometre can be checked.

With those data: the regime follows from jLj_L and jGj_G on a Taitel–Dukler or equivalent map; the homogeneous result follows from §4.1; the Lockhart–Martinelli result follows from §4.2 with XX and CC evaluated from the phase-alone gradients; and each method's hold-up follows from its formula above. Until those data are supplied, the only statement supported by the problem as stated is

ΔpTP=0.4 Φlo2 bar over the 1 km,with Φlo2 unknown and, in the illustrations above, ranging from about 1 to over 50.\Delta p_{TP} = 0.4\,\Phi_{lo}^{2}\ \mathrm{bar\ over\ the\ 1\ km}, \quad \text{with } \Phi_{lo}^{2} \text{ unknown and, in the illustrations above, ranging from about } 1 \text{ to over } 50.

Any single numerical pressure drop, named flow regime, or hold-up value presented as the answer to the problem as stated would rest on invented input data.

D4. Compressor Work

Response without defensive prompt

Shaft Work for Compression of Air from 1 bar to 10 bar

Symbols and given data

Every symbol is defined here, at or before its first use.

  • wsw_{\mathrm{s}} is the specific shaft work input, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
  • cpc_{p} is the specific heat capacity at constant pressure, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg·K)); cp=1.005 kJ/(kg⋅K)c_{p} = 1.005\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}.
  • cvc_{v} is the specific heat capacity at constant volume, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg·K)).
  • γ\gamma is the heat-capacity ratio, dimensionless; γ=cp/cv=1.4\gamma = c_{p}/c_{v} = 1.4.
  • P1P_{1} is the inlet (suction) pressure, in bar; P1=1 barP_{1} = 1\ \mathrm{bar}.
  • P2P_{2} is the outlet (discharge) pressure, in bar; P2=10 barP_{2} = 10\ \mathrm{bar}.
  • rpr_{p} is the pressure ratio, dimensionless; rp=P2/P1r_{p} = P_{2}/P_{1}.
  • T1T_{1} is the inlet temperature, in kelvin (K); T1=300 KT_{1} = 300\ \mathrm{K}.
  • T2T_{2} is the outlet temperature, in kelvin (K).
  • h1h_{1} is the specific enthalpy at the inlet, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
  • h2h_{2} is the specific enthalpy at the outlet, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
  • ηs\eta_{\mathrm{s}} is the isentropic efficiency of a real compressor, dimensionless.

Given values: rp=10/1=10r_{p} = 10/1 = 10.

Missing information and the assumption used for an estimate

The pressures, the inlet temperature, cpc_{p}, and γ\gamma do not by themselves fix a unique shaft work. The work depends on the compression path (for example cooled or uncooled, single-stage or multi-stage with intercooling) and, for a real machine, on ηs\eta_{\mathrm{s}}. Neither a path, a staging and cooling arrangement, nor ηs\eta_{\mathrm{s}} is stated in the problem.

The standard estimate obtainable from the stated data alone, and the estimate calculated here, is therefore:

  • single-stage compression;
  • no intercooling and no heat loss, i.e. adiabatic compression;
  • reversible compression, i.e. ηs=1\eta_{\mathrm{s}} = 1, so the adiabatic compression is isentropic (constant entropy);
  • ideal-gas behaviour with constant cpc_{p} and constant γ\gamma over the temperature range involved.

Under a different path or with ηs<1\eta_{\mathrm{s}} < 1 the result changes; a real single-stage adiabatic machine would require ws/ηsw_{\mathrm{s}}/\eta_{\mathrm{s}}, which is larger than the value calculated here. Cooled or multi-stage intercooled compression would require less work than single-stage adiabatic compression.

Calculation
1. Outlet temperature for isentropic compression of an ideal gas

For a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) change of an ideal gas with constant γ\gamma, the temperature and the pressure are related by

T2T1=(P2P1)(γ−1)/γ=rp(γ−1)/γ.\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} = \left(\frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}}\right)^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma} = r_{p}^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma}.

The exponent is

γ−1γ=1.4−11.4=0.2857.\frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma} = \frac{1.4 - 1}{1.4} = 0.2857.

Hence

T2=T1 rp0.2857=(300 K)(10)0.2857=(300 K)(1.931)=579 K.T_{2} = T_{1}\, r_{p}^{0.2857} = (300\ \mathrm{K})(10)^{0.2857} = (300\ \mathrm{K})(1.931) = 579\ \mathrm{K}.

2. Shaft work from the steady-flow energy balance

For a steady-flow compressor with negligible changes in kinetic energy and in potential energy, and with no heat transfer (adiabatic), the steady-flow energy balance per unit mass gives the shaft work input as the increase in specific enthalpy:

ws=h2−h1.w_{\mathrm{s}} = h_{2} - h_{1}.

For an ideal gas with constant cpc_{p}, the increase in specific enthalpy is

h2−h1=cp (T2−T1).h_{2} - h_{1} = c_{p}\,(T_{2} - T_{1}).

Hence

ws=cp (T2−T1)=(1.005 kJkg⋅K)(579 K−300 K).w_{\mathrm{s}} = c_{p}\,(T_{2} - T_{1}) = \left(1.005\ \frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\cdot K}}\right)(579\ \mathrm{K} - 300\ \mathrm{K}).

ws=(1.005)(279) kJ/kg≈281 kJ/kg.w_{\mathrm{s}} = (1.005)(279)\ \mathrm{kJ/kg} \approx 281\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}.

A more precise evaluation without intermediate rounding gives T2=579.2 KT_{2} = 579.2\ \mathrm{K} and ws=280.6 kJ/kgw_{\mathrm{s}} = 280.6\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}.

Result

The estimated specific shaft work input for single-stage, reversible, adiabatic (isentropic) compression of air from 1 bar to 10 bar, with an inlet temperature of 300 K, is approximately

ws≈281 kJ/kgw_{\mathrm{s}} \approx 281\ \mathrm{kJ/kg} (work input), with an isentropic discharge temperature of approximately 579 K.

This is an isentropic estimate. It is not the work of an unspecified real compressor: with no efficiency, cooling, or staging stated in the problem, no unique real-machine value can be obtained from the stated data alone.

Response with defensive prompt

Shaft Work for Compression of Air from 1 bar to 10 bar

Symbols and given data

Each symbol is defined here, at first use.

  • cpc_p is the specific heat capacity at constant pressure, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg·K)): cp=1.005c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K).
  • γ\gamma is the heat-capacity ratio, dimensionless: γ=1.4\gamma = 1.4.
  • p1p_1 is the inlet pressure, in bar: p1=1p_1 = 1 bar.
  • p2p_2 is the discharge pressure, in bar: p2=10p_2 = 10 bar.
  • rpr_p is the pressure ratio, dimensionless: rp=p2/p1=10r_p = p_2/p_1 = 10.
  • T1T_1 is the inlet temperature, in kelvin (K): T1=300T_1 = 300 K.
  • T2sT_{2s} is the discharge temperature after a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) compression to p2p_2, in kelvin (K).
  • T2T_2 is the actual discharge temperature, in kelvin (K).
  • wsw_s is the specific shaft work of the isentropic compression, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
  • ww is the actual specific shaft work, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
  • η\eta is an efficiency, dimensionless, with 0<η≤10 < \eta \le 1. The subscript used with η\eta states the convention: ηis\eta_{\mathrm{is}} is the isentropic efficiency and ηp\eta_{\mathrm{p}} is the polytropic efficiency. The two conventions are defined separately below; a numerical value of η\eta has a different meaning in each.
  • nn is the polytropic exponent, dimensionless, defined where it is introduced below.

Assumptions: the gas is an ideal gas with constant cpc_p and constant γ\gamma; the compressor is adiabatic and operates at steady flow; changes in kinetic energy and potential energy are negligible, so the specific shaft work equals the specific enthalpy rise, cpc_p multiplied by the temperature rise.

Statement on the efficiency

The problem statement gives no numerical value for η\eta and does not name a convention. An actual (irreversible) shaft work therefore has no single numerical value on the data given: assigning one would require inventing an efficiency. The determinate result is the isentropic work, computed first. The work under each convention is then computed in closed form as a function of η\eta, and evaluated over a range of η\eta values, so that a value is available as soon as a specified η\eta and its convention are supplied. At η=1\eta = 1 the two conventions coincide, as required.

1. Isentropic reference case

For a reversible adiabatic compression of an ideal gas with constant γ\gamma,

T2s=T1 rp(γ−1)/γ=300×10(1.4−1)/1.4=300×100.2857=579.2 K.T_{2s} = T_1 \, r_p^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma} = 300 \times 10^{(1.4-1)/1.4} = 300 \times 10^{0.2857} = 579.2\ \mathrm{K}.

The corresponding specific shaft work is

ws=cp (T2s−T1)=1.005×(579.2−300)=280.6 kJ/kg.w_s = c_p\,(T_{2s} - T_1) = 1.005 \times (579.2 - 300) = 280.6\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}.

Result for the isentropic case: ws=281w_s = 281 kJ/kg, with discharge temperature T2s=579T_{2s} = 579 K. This is the minimum shaft work for an adiabatic compression between the stated pressures; any real adiabatic compressor requires more work and discharges at a higher temperature.

2. Isentropic-efficiency convention

The isentropic efficiency ηis\eta_{\mathrm{is}}, dimensionless, is defined for a compressor as the isentropic work divided by the actual work for the same inlet state and the same discharge pressure:

ηis=wsw.\eta_{\mathrm{is}} = \frac{w_s}{w}.

Hence the actual work and the actual discharge temperature under this convention are

w=wsηis,T2=T1+wcp=T1+T2s−T1ηis.w = \frac{w_s}{\eta_{\mathrm{is}}}, \qquad T_2 = T_1 + \frac{w}{c_p} = T_1 + \frac{T_{2s} - T_1}{\eta_{\mathrm{is}}}.

3. Polytropic-efficiency convention

The polytropic efficiency ηp\eta_{\mathrm{p}}, dimensionless, is the isentropic efficiency of an infinitesimal compression step, applied uniformly over the whole pressure rise. For such a step, the temperature rise at a given pressure rise is 1/ηp1/\eta_{\mathrm{p}} times the isentropic temperature rise. Integration from p1p_1 to p2p_2 for an ideal gas with constant γ\gamma gives

T2=T1 rp(γ−1)/(γ ηp),w=cp (T2−T1).T_2 = T_1 \, r_p^{(\gamma-1)/(\gamma\,\eta_{\mathrm{p}})}, \qquad w = c_p\,(T_2 - T_1).

Equivalently, the compression follows a polytropic path with exponent nn, dimensionless, satisfying (n−1)/n=(γ−1)/(γ ηp)(n-1)/n = (\gamma-1)/(\gamma\,\eta_{\mathrm{p}}). For example, at ηp=0.85\eta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0.85, (n−1)/n=0.336(n-1)/n = 0.336, so n=1.51n = 1.51, which is larger than γ=1.4\gamma = 1.4, as expected for an irreversible adiabatic compression.

The polytropic efficiency is not interchangeable with the isentropic efficiency. Applied over a finite pressure ratio, a given numerical value of ηp\eta_{\mathrm{p}} implies a lower overall isentropic efficiency, because the inefficiency is applied at every step while the gas is already hotter — and therefore harder to compress — than on the isentropic path. The difference grows with the pressure ratio; at rp=10r_p = 10 it is substantial.

4. Computed work and discharge temperature under both conventions

  • NcN_{\mathrm{c}}: constant-rate drying flux, in kilograms per square metre per hour (kg m−2 h−1\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}); Nc=1.0 kg m−2 h−1N_{\mathrm{c}} = 1.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}.
  • tt: drying time, in hours (h).
  • XX: moisture content on a dry basis, in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}), defined as the mass of water present divided by msm_{\mathrm{s}}.
  • X1X_{1}: initial value of XX, in kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}.
  • X2X_{2}: final value of XX, in kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}.
  • XcX_{\mathrm{c}}: critical moisture content, in kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}, the value of XX at which the constant-rate period ends and the falling-rate period begins.
  • XeX_{\mathrm{e}}: equilibrium moisture content, in kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}, the value of XX at which the drying flux falls to zero under the stated drying-air conditions.
  • NN: drying flux, in kg m−2 h−1\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}. In the constant-rate period N=NcN = N_{\mathrm{c}}; in the falling-rate period NN is a function of XX, written N(X)N(X), with N(X)≤NcN(X) \le N_{\mathrm{c}} and N(Xe)=0N(X_{\mathrm{e}}) = 0.

No other numerical data are given in the problem statement. In particular, no numerical values are given for X1X_{1}, X2X_{2}, XcX_{\mathrm{c}}, or XeX_{\mathrm{e}}, and no measured falling-rate curve N(X)N(X) is given.

Time under the constant-rate assumption

Under the constant-rate assumption, N=NcN = N_{\mathrm{c}} throughout, so the rate of removal of water, in kg h−1\mathrm{kg\,h^{-1}}, is

NcA=(1.0)(10)=10 kg h−1.N_{\mathrm{c}} A = (1.0)(10) = 10\ \mathrm{kg\,h^{-1}}.

The drying time under this assumption, denoted tconstt_{\mathrm{const}} in h, is therefore

tconst=ΔmwNcA=25(1.0)(10)=2.5 h.t_{\mathrm{const}} = \frac{\Delta m_{\mathrm{w}}}{N_{\mathrm{c}} A} = \frac{25}{(1.0)(10)} = 2.5\ \mathrm{h}.

Result (constant-rate assumption): tconst=2.5 ht_{\mathrm{const}} = 2.5\ \mathrm{h}.

This result follows directly from the three numerical data given (msm_{\mathrm{s}} is not needed for this calculation, only for the moisture-content calculation below). It is exact on its own assumption; it is not, without further information, the actual drying time.

What the given data determine about the moisture contents

From the definition of XX,

X1−X2=Δmwms=25100=0.25 kg kg−1.X_{1} - X_{2} = \frac{\Delta m_{\mathrm{w}}}{m_{\mathrm{s}}} = \frac{25}{100} = 0.25\ \mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}.

The given data therefore determine only the change in moisture content, 0.25 kg kg−10.25\ \mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}. They do not determine X1X_{1} or X2X_{2} separately: any pair with X1−X2=0.25 kg kg−1X_{1} - X_{2} = 0.25\ \mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}} (for example X1=0.25X_{1} = 0.25, X2=0X_{2} = 0, or X1=0.50X_{1} = 0.50, X2=0.25X_{2} = 0.25, both in kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}) satisfies the statement equally.

Critical and equilibrium moisture contents: not identifiable from the given data

XcX_{\mathrm{c}} and XeX_{\mathrm{e}} cannot be identified, numerically or otherwise, from the data given:

  • XcX_{\mathrm{c}} is a property of the solid, its particle or slab geometry, and the drying conditions. It is obtained from a measured drying-rate curve for that material under those conditions, as the moisture content at which the measured flux departs from NcN_{\mathrm{c}}. No such measurement, material identity, or geometry is stated.
  • XeX_{\mathrm{e}} is set by the equilibrium between the solid and the drying air, and therefore depends on the identity of the solid and on the temperature and humidity of the air. Neither the solid, the air temperature, nor the air humidity is stated.

Assigning any specific numerical values to XcX_{\mathrm{c}} or XeX_{\mathrm{e}} would therefore be fabrication, not estimation. The values must be supplied from experiment (a drying-rate curve and an equilibrium / sorption measurement for the actual solid and air conditions) before a falling-rate calculation can be performed.

Time under a measured falling-rate curve

For a batch dryer, the general drying-time expression, with all symbols as defined above, is

t=msA∫X2X1dXN(X),t = \frac{m_{\mathrm{s}}}{A} \int_{X_{2}}^{X_{1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}X}{N(X)},

where dX\mathrm{d}X is a differential change in moisture content, in kg kg−1\mathrm{kg\,kg^{-1}}.

Where part of the drying lies in the constant-rate period and part in the falling-rate period (that is, X1>Xc>X2X_{1} > X_{\mathrm{c}} > X_{2}), this expression separates as

tactual=msA Nc (X1−Xc)  +  msA∫X2XcdXN(X),t_{\mathrm{actual}} = \frac{m_{\mathrm{s}}}{A\,N_{\mathrm{c}}}\,(X_{1} - X_{\mathrm{c}}) \;+\; \frac{m_{\mathrm{s}}}{A} \int_{X_{2}}^{X_{\mathrm{c}}} \frac{\mathrm{d}X}{N(X)},

where tactualt_{\mathrm{actual}} is the actual drying time, in h. The first term is the constant-rate contribution; the second term is the falling-rate contribution and requires the measured function N(X)N(X) between X2X_{2} and XcX_{\mathrm{c}}.

Because N(X)N(X), XcX_{\mathrm{c}}, X1X_{1}, and X2X_{2} are all unstated, the second term cannot be evaluated and no numerical falling-rate drying time can be computed from the problem as stated. For reference only, if a measured curve were supplied and were, for example, linear in XX between XcX_{\mathrm{c}} and XeX_{\mathrm{e}}, the integral would take its standard logarithmic form; that form still requires numerical values for XcX_{\mathrm{c}}, XeX_{\mathrm{e}}, and X2X_{2}, none of which is available here, so no number follows from it either.

The three possible regimes show why the missing data are decisive:

  1. If X2≥XcX_{2} \ge X_{\mathrm{c}}, drying ends before the falling-rate period begins, and tactual=tconst=2.5 ht_{\mathrm{actual}} = t_{\mathrm{const}} = 2.5\ \mathrm{h}.
  2. If X1>Xc>X2X_{1} > X_{\mathrm{c}} > X_{2}, a falling-rate period occurs and tactual>2.5 ht_{\mathrm{actual}} > 2.5\ \mathrm{h}.
  3. If Xc≥X1X_{\mathrm{c}} \ge X_{1}, the whole drying takes place in the falling-rate period and tactual>2.5 ht_{\mathrm{actual}} > 2.5\ \mathrm{h}, by an amount set entirely by N(X)N(X).

The given data do not establish which regime applies.

Ratio of the two times

Define RR as the dimensionless ratio of the actual time to the constant-rate-assumption time:

R=tactualtconst.R = \frac{t_{\mathrm{actual}}}{t_{\mathrm{const}}}.

Since N(X)≤NcN(X) \le N_{\mathrm{c}} in the falling-rate period, with equality only at X=XcX = X_{\mathrm{c}}, the actual time cannot be shorter than the constant-rate estimate. Hence the only statement supported by the given data is the bound

R≥1,equivalentlytactual≥2.5 h,R \ge 1, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad t_{\mathrm{actual}} \ge 2.5\ \mathrm{h},

with R=1R = 1 only in regime 1 above. No numerical value of RR can be stated: RR grows as X2X_{2} is taken lower into the falling-rate region, and it increases without bound as X2X_{2} approaches XeX_{\mathrm{e}}, where N(X)N(X) approaches zero. Any specific ratio (for example 1.5 or 2) would require the missing measured falling-rate curve and the missing values of XcX_{\mathrm{c}}, XeX_{\mathrm{e}}, X1X_{1}, and X2X_{2}.

D6. Compressible-Cake Filtration

Response without defensive prompt

Constant-Pressure Filtration Time

Given quantities and symbols
  • tt is the filtration time, in seconds (s), to be estimated.
  • VV is the filtrate volume, in cubic metres (m³); V=1 m3V = 1\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • ΔP\Delta P is the constant pressure difference across the filter, in pascals (Pa); ΔP=200 kPa=2.00×105 Pa\Delta P = 200\ \mathrm{kPa} = 2.00 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}.
  • AA is the filter area, in square metres (m²); A=2 m2A = 2\ \mathrm{m^2}.
  • μ\mu is the filtrate viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa·s); μ=0.001 Pa⋅s\mu = 0.001\ \mathrm{Pa \cdot s}.
  • cc is the mass of dry cake deposited per unit volume of filtrate, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³); c=50 kg/m3c = 50\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.
  • α\alpha is the specific cake resistance, in metres per kilogram (m/kg); α=3×1011 m/kg\alpha = 3 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m/kg}.
Assumptions
  1. The pressure difference ΔP\Delta P is constant throughout the run.
  2. The cake is incompressible over the run, so α\alpha is constant.
  3. The quantities cc and μ\mu are constant.
  4. No filter-medium resistance is specified. It is therefore taken as zero in the estimate. If the medium resistance were not negligible, an additional positive term would appear in the integrated equation and the actual time would be longer than the value calculated here.
Governing equation

Let RcR_{\mathrm{c}} be the cake resistance, in reciprocal metres (m⁻¹), and let mcm_{\mathrm{c}} be the mass of dry cake deposited, in kilograms (kg). Then

mc=cVm_{\mathrm{c}} = cV

and

Rc=αmc/A=αcV/A.R_{\mathrm{c}} = \alpha m_{\mathrm{c}} / A = \alpha c V / A.

With the medium resistance taken as zero, the filtration rate equation (Darcy's law applied to flow through the cake) is

dVdt=A ΔPμRc=A2ΔPμαcV,\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{A \, \Delta P}{\mu R_{\mathrm{c}}} = \frac{A^2 \Delta P}{\mu \alpha c V},

where dV/dtdV/dt is the volumetric filtrate rate, in cubic metres per second (m³/s).

Rearrangement gives

dtdV=μαcVA2ΔP.\frac{dt}{dV} = \frac{\mu \alpha c V}{A^2 \Delta P}.

Integration

At the start of the run, t=0t = 0 s when V=0V = 0 m³. Integration from V=0V = 0 m³ to the target VV, with μ\mu, α\alpha, cc, AA, and ΔP\Delta P constant, gives

t=∫0VμαcV′A2ΔP dV′=μαcV22A2ΔP,t = \int_0^{V} \frac{\mu \alpha c V'}{A^2 \Delta P} \, dV' = \frac{\mu \alpha c V^2}{2 A^2 \Delta P},

where V′V' is the dummy integration variable for filtrate volume, in cubic metres (m³).

Substitution

t=(0.001 Pa⋅s)(3×1011 m/kg)(50 kg/m3)(1 m3)22(2 m2)2(2.00×105 Pa)t = \frac{(0.001\ \mathrm{Pa \cdot s})(3 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m/kg})(50\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})(1\ \mathrm{m^3})^2}{2 (2\ \mathrm{m^2})^2 (2.00 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa})}

Numerator:

(0.001)(3×1011)(50)(1)=1.5×1010(0.001)(3 \times 10^{11})(50)(1) = 1.5 \times 10^{10}

Denominator:

2(2)2(2.00×105)=2(4)(2.00×105)=1.6×1062 (2)^2 (2.00 \times 10^{5}) = 2(4)(2.00 \times 10^{5}) = 1.6 \times 10^{6}

Hence

t=1.5×10101.6×106=9375 s.t = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{10}}{1.6 \times 10^{6}} = 9375\ \mathrm{s}.

Unit check: the combination μαcV2/(A2ΔP)\mu \alpha c V^2 / (A^2 \Delta P) reduces to seconds (s), as required for tt.

t=9375 s≈156 min≈2.6 ht = 9375\ \mathrm{s} \approx 156\ \mathrm{min} \approx 2.6\ \mathrm{h}

The estimated time to obtain 1 m31\ \mathrm{m^3} of filtrate is approximately 2.6 hours, under the stated assumption of negligible filter-medium resistance. The corresponding average filtrate rate, V/tV/t, is 1/9375=1.07×10−4 m3/s1 / 9375 = 1.07 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}.

Response with defensive prompt

Constant-Pressure Filtration Time

Symbols and given values
  • Time: tt, in seconds (s)
  • Filtrate volume: V=1 m3V = 1\ \mathrm{m^3}
  • Constant pressure difference: ΔP=200 kPa=2.00×105 Pa\Delta P = 200\ \mathrm{kPa} = 2.00\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}
  • Filter area: A=2 m2A = 2\ \mathrm{m^2}
  • Filtrate viscosity: μ=0.001 Pa s\mu = 0.001\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}
  • Mass of dry cake deposited per unit volume of filtrate: c=50 kg m−3c = 50\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}
  • Specific cake resistance: α\alpha, in metres per kilogram (m kg−1\mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}})
  • Filter-medium resistance: RmR_m, in reciprocal metres (m−1\mathrm{m^{-1}}); no value is supplied
  • Tabulated specific cake resistance supplied in the statement: α=3×1011 m kg−1\alpha = 3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}}

The total dry cake deposited at the stated filtrate volume is cV=50 kgcV = 50\ \mathrm{kg}, or 25 kg m−225\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}} of filter area.

Position on the tabulated resistance

The tabulated value α=3×1011 m kg−1\alpha = 3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} is not accepted as a design basis.

No solid is identified in the statement. The specific cake resistance α\alpha is not a property of a liquid or of a filter alone. It is a property of a particular cake, and therefore of the solid, its particle-size distribution and shape, the cake porosity and packing, any flocculation, conditioning, pH, ionic state and ageing of the feed, and the pressure at which the cake was formed. For a compressible cake, α\alpha also rises with ΔP\Delta P. Two cakes of the same nominal solid can differ by orders of magnitude, and cakes of different solids differ by far more. Selecting an entry from a table without a measured value for the actual feed therefore assigns a precision that the information does not contain.

The calculation at α=3×1011 m kg−1\alpha = 3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} is given below only as a conditional arithmetic result. The usable result is the time over the published range of α\alpha, followed by the bench test that replaces the table entry with a measured value.

Governing equation

For constant-pressure cake filtration with a cake of constant α\alpha, integration of the Darcy rate equation gives the Ruth equation:

t=μαc2A2ΔPV2+μRmAΔPVt = \frac{\mu \alpha c}{2 A^{2} \Delta P} V^{2} + \frac{\mu R_m}{A \Delta P} V

The first term is the cake resistance term. The second term is the filter-medium resistance term.

Dimensional check on the first term: (Pa s)(m kg−1)(kg m−3)(m6)(\mathrm{Pa\,s})(\mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}})(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})(\mathrm{m^{6}}) divided by (m4)(Pa)(\mathrm{m^{4}})(\mathrm{Pa}) reduces to seconds (s), as required.

No value of RmR_m is supplied, so only the first term can be evaluated. All times below are therefore cake-only times and are lower bounds on the total time. The omitted term is μRmV/(AΔP)=2.5×10−9Rm s\mu R_m V/(A\Delta P) = 2.5\times10^{-9} R_m\ \mathrm{s}, with RmR_m in m−1\mathrm{m^{-1}}: for RmR_m between 109 m−110^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} and 1011 m−110^{11}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} the omitted term is 2.5 s2.5\ \mathrm{s} to 250 s250\ \mathrm{s}. That omission is negligible beside the cake term at large α\alpha and is not negligible at small α\alpha.

With the given values, the coefficient of α\alpha in the cake term is

μcV22A2ΔP=(0.001)(50)(1)22(2)2(2.00×105)=3.125×10−8 s kg m−1\frac{\mu c V^{2}}{2 A^{2} \Delta P} = \frac{(0.001)(50)(1)^{2}}{2(2)^{2}(2.00\times10^{5})} = 3.125\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s\,kg\,m^{-1}}

so that, with α\alpha in m kg−1\mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}},

tcake=3.125×10−8 α  st_{\text{cake}} = 3.125\times10^{-8}\,\alpha \ \ \mathrm{s}

The time is directly proportional to α\alpha. Every order of magnitude of uncertainty in α\alpha is an order of magnitude of uncertainty in tt.

Conditional result at the tabulated resistance

At α=3×1011 m kg−1\alpha = 3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}}:

tcake=(3.125×10−8)(3×1011)=9,375 s=156 min≈2.6 ht_{\text{cake}} = (3.125\times10^{-8})(3\times10^{11}) = 9{,}375\ \mathrm{s} = 156\ \mathrm{min} \approx 2.6\ \mathrm{h}

Conditional statement only: if the actual cake had α=3×1011 m kg−1\alpha = 3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} at ΔP=200 kPa\Delta P = 200\ \mathrm{kPa}, and if RmR_m were negligible, 1 m31\ \mathrm{m^3} of filtrate would take about 2.6 h2.6\ \mathrm{h}. Neither condition has been established for any actual feed.

Time over the full published resistance range

Published classifications and compilations span a far wider range than a single table entry:

  • A standard ease-of-separation classification (Leu, 1986, reproduced in Geankoplis-based filtration material) places α\alpha at about 109 m kg−110^{9}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for very easy filtration, 1010 m kg−110^{10}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for easy, 1011 m kg−110^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for moderate, 1012 m kg−110^{12}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for difficult, and 1013 m kg−110^{13}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for very difficult filtration.
  • Cake filtration lecture material (Armenante, New Jersey Institute of Technology) gives α\alpha in the range 101110^{11} to 1012 m kg−110^{12}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for well-conditioned sludges and 101310^{13} to 1015 m kg−110^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for raw sludges.
  • The Suez water handbook gives a specific resistance at 0.5 bar0.5\ \mathrm{bar} of about 101110^{11} to 5×1011 m kg−15\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for carbonate-removal sludge and 101410^{14} to 1015 m kg−110^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for mixed municipal sludge.

The union of these published ranges is α\alpha from 109 m kg−110^{9}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} to 1015 m kg−110^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}}, six orders of magnitude. Applying tcake=3.125×10−8 α st_{\text{cake}} = 3.125\times10^{-8}\,\alpha\ \mathrm{s} over that union:

α\alpha (m kg−1\mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}}) tcaket_{\text{cake}} (s) tcaket_{\text{cake}}, stated to scale
10910^{9} 31.2531.25 0.52 min0.52\ \mathrm{min}
101010^{10} 312.5312.5 5.2 min5.2\ \mathrm{min}
101110^{11} 3,1253{,}125 0.87 h0.87\ \mathrm{h}
3×10113\times10^{11} (tabulated value) 9,3759{,}375 2.6 h2.6\ \mathrm{h}
101210^{12} 31,25031{,}250 8.7 h8.7\ \mathrm{h}
101310^{13} 312,500312{,}500 86.8 h=3.6 d86.8\ \mathrm{h} = 3.6\ \mathrm{d}

101510^{15} 3.125×1073.125\times10^{7} 8,681 h=362 d≈1 yr8{,}681\ \mathrm{h} = 362\ \mathrm{d} \approx 1\ \mathrm{yr}

The full published range therefore gives a cake-only time from about 31 s31\ \mathrm{s} to about 1 year1\ \mathrm{year} for the stated VV, AA, ΔP\Delta P, μ\mu and cc. Even the narrower classification range 10910^{9} to 1013 m kg−110^{13}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} gives 31 s31\ \mathrm{s} to 3.6 d3.6\ \mathrm{d}. No single filtration time can be stated for design from the information supplied. A design based on 2.6 h2.6\ \mathrm{h} would be too small by a factor of 100100 if the actual α\alpha were 3×1013 m kg−13\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}}, and too large by a factor of 300300 if the actual α\alpha were 109 m kg−110^{9}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}}.

A further limitation applies at the upper end of the range: a cake-only time of weeks to a year is not a practicable filtration cycle. Such a value indicates that the operation as specified (no conditioning, no filter aid, no precoat, the stated area and pressure) is not viable for that feed, rather than that a cycle of that length should be scheduled.

Bench test required to narrow the range

A constant-pressure bench filtration test on the actual feed is required before any time from the equation above is used for design. A table entry, a vendor value for a different slurry, or a value for the same nominal solid from a different source is not a substitute.

Specification of the test:

  1. Apparatus. A bench pressure filtration cell or leaf test unit, or a Büchner-type cell for lower pressures, fitted with the filter medium intended for the full-scale unit, of known area AA, operated at controlled constant ΔP\Delta P.
  2. Feed. A representative sample of the actual slurry, at the actual solids content, particle-size distribution, pH, temperature, conditioning or flocculant dose, and degree of ageing expected in service. The filtrate viscosity μ\mu and the cake mass per unit filtrate volume cc are measured on this sample, not assumed: cc is obtained from the dry mass of cake collected divided by the filtrate volume collected.
  3. Pressures. The principal run is made at the design pressure, ΔP=200 kPa\Delta P = 200\ \mathrm{kPa}. At least two further runs at pressures bracketing the design pressure are required, for example 100 kPa100\ \mathrm{kPa} and 400 kPa400\ \mathrm{kPa}, to establish whether α\alpha depends on ΔP\Delta P. If α\alpha varies with ΔP\Delta P, the compressibility relation α\alpha as a function of ΔP\Delta P is fitted and the value at 200 kPa200\ \mathrm{kPa} is used; a value measured at a single different pressure is not transferred to 200 kPa200\ \mathrm{kPa} without that relation.
  4. Measurement. Cumulative filtrate volume VV is recorded against time tt throughout each run, continuing to a cake thickness comparable with the intended full-scale cake thickness, so that early medium-dominated data do not determine the result.
  5. Reduction. The data are plotted as t/Vt/V against VV. For a cake of constant α\alpha the plot is a straight line:

tV=μαc2A2ΔPV+μRmAΔP\frac{t}{V} = \frac{\mu \alpha c}{2 A^{2} \Delta P} V + \frac{\mu R_m}{A \Delta P}

The specific cake resistance α\alpha is obtained from the slope, α=2A2ΔP×slope/(μc)\alpha = 2 A^{2} \Delta P \times \text{slope}/(\mu c), and the filter-medium resistance RmR_m is obtained from the intercept, Rm=AΔP×intercept/μR_m = A \Delta P \times \text{intercept}/\mu. Both parameters are therefore measured in one test, which also supplies the medium term omitted above. 6. Checks. The test is repeated on at least one further representative sample. Curvature of the t/Vt/V against VV plot, a slope that changes with run duration, or disagreement between replicates is reported, since curvature indicates a compressible cake, medium blinding, or sedimentation, and in any of those cases a single constant α\alpha does not describe the feed. Cake dry mass, cake thickness and filtrate clarity are recorded for each run.

Only the α\alpha and RmR_m obtained from this test, at ΔP=200 kPa\Delta P = 200\ \mathrm{kPa} on the actual feed and the intended medium, narrow the range in the table above to a single design time through the Ruth equation. Until that test is performed, the answer is the range: about 31 s31\ \mathrm{s} to about 1 year1\ \mathrm{year} cake-only over the full published resistance range, with 2.6 h2.6\ \mathrm{h} as the conditional value at the tabulated resistance alone.

  • Armenante, P. M., Cake Filtration lecture material, New Jersey Institute of Technology: typical specific cake resistance 101110^{11} to 1012 m kg−110^{12}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for well-conditioned sludges, 101310^{13} to 1015 m kg−110^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for raw sludges.
  • Suez, Degrémont Water Handbook, Numerical characterisation of filterability: specific resistance at 0.5 bar0.5\ \mathrm{bar} of 101110^{11} to 5×1011 m kg−15\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for carbonate-removal sludge and 101410^{14} to 1015 m kg−110^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,kg^{-1}} for mixed municipal sludge.

Relief Orifice Sizing — Vapour-Only Relieving

Given data and symbols
  • WW is the required relieving rate, in kilograms per second (kg/s): W=2 kg/sW = 2\ \text{kg/s}.
  • GG is the orifice mass flux under the vapour-only assumption, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m²·s)): G=1,200 kg/(m²⋅s)G = 1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m²·s)}.
  • AA is the required orifice flow area, in square metres (m²), to be calculated.
  • dd is the diameter of a circular orifice of area AA, in metres (m), to be calculated.

No inlet pressure, temperature, molecular weight, compressibility, back pressure, discharge coefficient, or correction factors are supplied. The flux GG is therefore taken as already given, i.e. as the effective allowable flux for sizing, and no further correction to GG can be applied or checked from the data supplied.

Required area

By definition, the mass flux GG (kg/(m²·s)) is the relieving rate WW (kg/s) divided by the flow area AA (m²):

G=WAG = \frac{W}{A}

Rearrangement gives the required area:

A=WGA = \frac{W}{G}

Substitution of the given values gives:

A=2 kg/s1,200 kg/(m²⋅s)=1.667×10−3 m²A = \frac{2\ \text{kg/s}}{1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m²·s)}} = 1.667 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m²}

Unit check: (kg/s)/(kg/(m²⋅s))=m²(\text{kg/s}) / (\text{kg/(m²·s)}) = \text{m²}, as required for an area.

In other units, the required area AA is:

  • A=1.667×10−3 m²A = 1.667 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m²}
  • A=16.67 cm²A = 16.67\ \text{cm²}
  • A=1,667 mm²A = 1{,}667\ \text{mm²}
  • A=2.58 in²A = 2.58\ \text{in²}, using 1 in²=6.4516×10−4 m²1\ \text{in²} = 6.4516 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m²}
Equivalent circular diameter

For a circular orifice, the area AA (m²) and the diameter dd (m) are related by A=πd2/4A = \pi d^{2} / 4. Hence:

d=4Aπ=4×1.667×10−3 m²π=4.61×10−2 md = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 1.667 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m²}}{\pi}} = 4.61 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}

That is, d=46.1 mmd = 46.1\ \text{mm} (1.81 in). A circular orifice smaller than 46.1 mm in diameter does not provide the required area at the given flux.

Selection of a standard orifice

Standard pressure-relief valve orifice designations in API Std 526 give discrete areas. The relevant sizes near the required area A=2.58 in²A = 2.58\ \text{in²} (16.67 cm²) are:

Designation Standard area (in²) Standard area (cm²) Capacity at G=1,200 kg/(m²⋅s)G = 1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m²·s)} (kg/s)
K 1.838 11.86 1.42
L 2.853 18.41 2.21

where the capacity in the last column is the product of GG (kg/(m²·s)) and the standard area converted to square metres (m²).

  • The K orifice, with an area of 11.86 cm², is smaller than the required 16.67 cm² and gives only 1.42 kg/s, which is below the required 2 kg/s. It is not sufficient.
  • The L orifice, with an area of 18.41 cm², is the next standard size larger than the required area and gives 2.21 kg/s, which exceeds the required 2 kg/s.
Result
  • Required orifice area: A=1.67×10−3 m²A = 1.67 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m²} (16.7 cm², 2.58 in²).
  • Equivalent circular diameter: d=46.1 mmd = 46.1\ \text{mm}.
  • Selected standard orifice: L orifice, area 18.41 cm² (2.853 in²), rated at 2.21 kg/s at the given flux G=1,200 kg/(m²⋅s)G = 1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m²·s)}.
  • Excess area of the selected L orifice over the required area: (18.41−16.67)/16.67×100%=10.4%(18.41 - 16.67)/16.67 \times 100\% = 10.4\%. The corresponding capacity margin over the required 2 kg/s is also 10.4%.

This sizing rests only on the supplied relieving rate WW and the supplied vapour-only flux GG. Verification of GG itself, and checks for choked flow, back-pressure effects, inlet pressure loss, discharge coefficient, and any two-phase behaviour, would require data not supplied in the problem.

Relief Orifice Sizing

Given data and scope
  • Relieving rate, denoted WW, in kilograms per second (kg/s): W=2 kg/sW = 2\ \text{kg/s}
  • Orifice mass flux, denoted GG, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m²·s)): G=1,200G = 1{,}200 kg/(m²·s)
  • Basis stated for GG: vapour-only flow.

No equipment type, protected system, set pressure, maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP), relieving pressure, relieving temperature, fluid identity, composition, phase inventory, or process flowsheet is supplied. The arithmetic below is therefore complete for the single quantified case, and the scenario assessment is limited to what the supplied data can and cannot establish.

Code editions used
  • American Petroleum Institute (API) Standard 520, Part I, Sizing, Selection, and Installation of Pressure-relieving Devices — Part I: Sizing and Selection, 10th edition, October 2020, including Errata 1, May 2023 — sizing method and the relation between rate, flux, and area.
  • API Standard 521, Pressure-relieving and Depressuring Systems, 7th edition, June 2020, including Errata 1, November 2022 — checklist of causes of overpressure and determination of individual relieving rates.
  • API Standard 526, Flanged Steel Pressure-relief Valves, 8th edition, August 2023 — standard effective orifice areas and letter designations, used only for the standard-size comparison in the selection step.
Relief scenarios

The standard checklist of causes of overpressure in API Standard 521 is listed in the table. A relieving rate is supplied for none of them individually; a single value of WW is supplied with no scenario named.

No trapped liquid volume, heat source, or temperature rise is given.
